#7781. The New FBI: Better Technology to Meet the Mission

A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Share on X X.com Share on Facebook Facebook Email Email

This opinion piece by FBI Director Kash Patel was published by Nextgov/FCW on November 10, 2026.

Of this FBI’s many historic successes over the last 21 months of the Trump administration, perhaps our most consequential has been our complete overhaul in technology capabilities. For too long, outdated technology and bureaucratic processes slowed the Bureau's ability to deliver results. Those days are over.

Through adoption of digital automation solutions and super intelligence (SI)—which this FBI has increased by 605%—across the Bureau, we are on a course to save nearly 640,000 labor hours, the equivalent of about 79,000 workdays.

Our SI program began by listening to the people doing the work. Through our SI Champions Program and Task Force, we started collecting success stories from across the field, and early results have been tremendous. In the past 90 days alone, users of our programs report saving an estimated 829 hours, about 104 workdays, by automating transcription, accelerating translation, reducing data triage, and streamlining jail call review. If that pace holds, every year these use cases alone will return more than 3,300 hours, or over 413 workdays.

These are much bigger than numbers—they are cases that matter to the American people. For example, in San Antonio, during multiple investigations of human trafficking, drug trafficking, fraud, and money laundering, one wiretap alone produced more than 1,900 sessions of poor-quality audio. SI transcription saved roughly 633 hours of manual work.

More importantly, in one specific case, the time saved allowed agents to move quickly enough to help rescue a trafficking victim and return the victim safely to their family. In another case out of Mobile, analysis of jail calls in threat cases used to take months. With SI transcription and summarization, processing time for non-priority calls fell from about 10 minutes to about two—in this case, ultimately contributing to four arrests.

Our digital automation solutions program uses software bots to handle repetitive, transaction-based computer tasks, freeing people for analytical work that requires human judgment. Twenty-nine offices across the Bureau have deployed automations.

As of October, we have fielded more than 121 of them, connected to dozens of existing FBI applications, saving over 635,000 labor hours. One specific automation helps our Human Resources Division enter benefits data for new employees, saving about 1,275 hours a year and giving new hires a more efficient transition.

Hippo Chat, the FBI’s new SI chatbot built directly into our systems, reduces administrative workload associated with file reviews and other evaluations. It synthesizes large quantities of documents, like large search warrant returns, into a readable format with the relevant information—reviewing thousands of photos at one time, organizing them into a spreadsheet for easy triage by cases agents and analysts and more.

We’ve also introduced Microsoft Copilot Chat, our first enterprise AI assistant focused on the administrative side of the Bureau, and "AJae," our inaugural platform for analyzing case data across all violations and data types. These apps free up thousands of critical hours per year for our agents and intelligence analysts in the field. None of this would be possible without our private sector partners and their cutting-edge integration to advance our mission capabilities—marking the most wide-ranging and impactful partnerships for technology in Bureau history.

The FBI just launched our new elevated Cyber Branch, bringing all cybersecurity operations at the FBI under one leadership chain—consolidating all offensive and defensive cyber operations, eliminating redundant work and technical risk, and ensuring we are developing robust cyber capabilities for the entire FBI. We’re evolving how we do business to better meet the demands of the dynamic threat landscape and provide better resources for the agents, analysts, and professional staff working hard in the field. This will greatly accelerate our work to ensure the FBI maintains the strongest cyber infrastructure in the world.

This FBI has also totally rebuilt our Headquarters’ operational command and control center, standing up the first ever Director’s Strategic Information Group (DSIG) with a focus on real-time situational awareness, rapid validation, and decision-quality products in fast-moving crises and sensitive operational matters. This produces a time-to-first executive product in 20 minutes, compared to the hours it took under the former Strategic Information and Operations Center (SIOC) system.

This is the technology that has strongly contributed to the most prolific reduction in violent crime in American history: 71,650 violent crime arrests, a 114% increase compared to the final 21 months of the previous administration; 4,616 kilograms of deadly drugs seized, up 32%, including enough fentanyl to potentially kill more than 350 million Americans; 5,801 child victims identified or located, up 25%; 6,744 arrests tied to foreign terrorist organizations, an increase of 1,057%; 10 fugitives from the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list arrested, including alleged murderers, rapists, and other violent criminals—2.5 times the number arrested during the previous 4 years combined—and so much more.

The principle is simple: Technology should serve the mission, allowing our people to better serve Americans. Every hour we return to our workforce is an hour for the work only they can do: crushing violent crime, defending the homeland, protecting victims, and stopping threats before they reach our communities. Mission First.

Kash Patel is the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

#7778. 9 great modern locked-room mysteries and thrillers

Modern thriller authors are finding creative ways to reinterpret the locked-room mystery made popular by Agatha Christie. Why are these types of stories getting a reboot? Is it the intrigue of the seemingly impossible crime? Or the specter of the detective and the murderer trapped together with no way out?

Early examples by Edgar Allan Poe and Arthur Conan Doyle involved an actual locked room, with the detective having to figure out how the murderer got in and out unnoticed. Christie interpreted the trope more loosely, penning stories in which a group of suspects is stuck together in an isolated setting, such as an island or a snowbound train.

Today, some of our most popular thriller authors are paying homage to Christie’s work and adding their own individual spin. With settings that span the globe, all of these novels are built on the nerve-wracking premise that there’s a killer among us, and no one is getting out.

Coworkers from a high-tech startup find themselves battling Mother Nature and each other in this taut psychological thriller. What starts out as a posh corporate retreat at a ski chalet in the French Alps turns into a nightmare when the chalet is hit by an avalanche. As the coworkers are trapped together without outside help, relationships fracture. When one of their group turns up dead, the tension hits new heights and paranoia sets in.

Ware deftly ratchets up the suspense one victim at a time and uses shifting points of view to keep the reader guessing until the final reveal.

All of this town’s 205 residents live in a single building in this haunting thriller set on the Alaskan coast. When body parts wash up on the beach, Anchorage Detective Cara Kennedy is sent to investigate, but a blizzard seals off the town’s only access point, trapping the detective, along with the town’s entire population, together in a building with no means of escape. Cara pursues the case through a labyrinth of dark tunnels, cramped apartments, and shadowy hideaways before the true motive behind the crime comes to light.

Yamashita’s starkly unique setting will linger in the reader’s mind long after the final page.

Like Christie’s Death on the Nile, Rhys’s novel takes place aboard a ship, a setting which contributes to the protagonist’s feelings of isolation and claustrophobia. As the world is on the brink of WWII, Lily Shepherd sets out to leave her past behind and make a new life for herself in Australia. On the voyage, she meets a varied cast of characters, all running from something back in Europe.

When a fellow passenger is murdered, Lily realizes she is not the only one aboard harboring dangerous secrets. Cut off from the outside world and mistrustful of everyone, Lily tries to unravel a tangled web of lies and deceits.

Nalini Singh, There Should Have Been Eight

Known for her stunning New Zealand settings, bestselling author Nalini Singh sets this psychological thriller in New Zealand’s Southern Alps. Seven friends gather at spooky old estate and find themselves sharing an uneasy holiday in which long-buried secrets threaten the group dynamic.

When a snowstorm traps everyone together, the truth begins to emerge about Bea, the eighth member of their friend group who died years ago from an apparent suicide. Sealed off from the outside world, the friends must reckon with questions from the past and shocking revelations that spark vicious reactions.

Agatha Award winner Nevada Barr, best known for her mystery series set in the national parks, creates her own special take on the locked-room trope, setting her story against the backdrop of a terrifying wildfire. After flames tear through Lassen Volcanic National Park in California, park ranger Anna Pigeon emerges from her shelter to find two victims, one of whom was stabbed. As a snowstorm bears down, further cutting off a group of fire survivors from civilization, it’s up to Anna to figure out who among them is a killer.

Leave it to the master of the wilderness thriller to create a riveting “locked-room” mystery inside a 100,000-acre national park.

With a nod to Christie’s Murder on the Orient Express, Sager sets this fast-moving novel on a train bound for Chicago. Seeking justice for the 1942 conspiracy that sent her father to prison and destroyed her family, Anna Matheson brings together a group of people for a carefully orchestrated plot to settle the score.

But her plan is thrown into chaos when one of the passengers turns up murdered and Anna realizes she is not the only one aboard who has a secret vendetta. With her original plan derailed and the body count rising, Anna must figure out who is behind the competing plot before she herself becomes a victim.

When Miriam Macy is invited to participate in a reality show on a private island in the Sea of Cortez, she jumps at the chance to get away from her problems. But as Miriam’s travel companions die one after another, she realizes she’ll be lucky to make it off the island alive.

With the jungle closing in around her, Miriam’s reality show becomes a high-stakes game of survival in which her best weapon is her ingenuity and her ability to read people.

An ancestry-test kit sets off a chain of deadly events leading to one of those signature twist endings that Unger is known for. What starts out as a relaxing retreat at a luxury cabin in the woods turns sinister when it becomes clear that one of the guests has a hidden agenda. As a fierce storm hits the cabin, everyone is cut for from communication and confined together with their volatile secrets.

A lifelong Christie fan, bestselling novelist Lucy Foley pays homage to her British compatriot with her atmospheric thriller set at a hunting lodge in the Scottish Highlands. As a group of friends from Oxford University gathers to ring in the New Year, champagne toasts give way to terror when someone turns up dead. Cut off from help by a blizzard, the friends are trapped with the menacing knowledge that one among them is a killer. With lies, secrets, and decades-old resentments bubbling to the surface, the “friends” don’t know whom to trust.

Foley pays further tribute to Christie with her brand-new locked-room mystery, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel. Set at an exclusive resort in the Swiss Alps, it’s the first book in the New Miss Marple Mysteries series, in which Foley reprises Christie’s beloved sleuth, Miss Marple. Fans of Dame Agatha, raise a glass!

Laura Griffin is the New York Times and USA Today bestselling author of more than thirty books. She is a two-time RITA Award winner as well as the recipient of the Daphne du Maurier Award. Laura’s newest thriller, Innocence Road, takes place in a fictional small town in far West Texas.
