#7774. Jacob Elordi will star in an adaptation of The Executioner’s Song

Fresh off his Oscar-nominated turn as the Creature in Frankenstein, Jacob Elordi is set to star in and produce an adaptation of Norman Mailer’s Pulitzer prize-winning 1979 novel The Executioner’s Song.

The Executioner’s Song is a complex, fictionalizd biography-of-sorts of American murderer Gary Gilmore, who, after being convicted of murdering two men in Utah, insisted on his death penalty sentence being carried out, despite the national moratorium on capital punishment implemented by the Supreme Court case Furman v. Georgia, which decided that different states’ inconsistent approaches toward criminal execution violated the Eight and Fourteenth amendments. Gilmore, who fought anti-capital punishment attorneys insistent on preserving his life, was eventually executed by firing squad in 1977.

The novel is broken up into two sections: “Western Voices,” and “Eastern Voices.” The first part is about the forces that made Gilmore into the man he became (including a youth spent in child detention facilities in the barren American west), while the second is about the media frenzy and national debate around the case, and spotlights, in particular, Gilmore’s relationship with the celebrity photographer Lawrence “Larry” Schiller, who conducted many interviews with Gilmore, his family, and others related to the case and brought the project to Mailer, in the first place.

Mailer continued Schiller’s research to craft a nearly 1000-page, plainly-written epic about the nihilism of the American West, the American proclivity towards violence, media madness, the exploitation of the working class, and the cult of white male loneliness. In her review in The New York Times Book Review, Joan Didion raved about Mailer’s accomplishment, calling it “an absolutely astonishing book,” and noting how it shocked her by being about something much more than what it initially seemed: “The Executioner’s Song did not suggest, in its inception, the book it became,” she wrote. “It began as a project put together by Lawrence Schiller, the photographer and producer who several years before had contracted with Mailer to write “Marilyn,” and it was widely referred to as ‘the Gary Gilmore book.’

It seemed one of those lives in which the narrative would yield no further meaning… What Mailer could make of this apparently intractable material was unclear. It might well have been only another test hole in a field he had drilled before, a few further reflections on murder as an existential act, an appropriation for himself of the book he invented for An American Dream, Stephen Rojack’s The Psychology of the Hangman. Instead Mailer wrote a novel, a thousand-page novel in a meticulously limited vocabulary and a voice as flat as the horizon, a novel which takes for its incident and characters real events in the lives of real people.

What she found instead, she writes, was a novel telling a story of a uniquely American desperation. She marvels at how Mailer uses his sentences to convey this above all else: the countless failed attempts for relatedness between people and things, with the sparseness of his prose summoning a “search for a field of negative energy linking these events and these people and the empty melancholy of the place itself.”

She also notes, with surprise, that the strongest of the novel’s voices are the women: “Men tend to shoot, get shot, push off, move on. Women pass down stories.”

Schiller and Mailer had collaborated as photographer-and-writer on numerous projects, beginning with 1972’s Marilyn: a Biography, and The Executioner’s Song is unquestionably their most monumental. Schiller, who directed the 1982 film adaptation of the novel starring Tommy Lee Jones, will executive-produce the new adaptation.

Elordi, who rose to stardom in HBO’s Euphoria, will play Gilmore (a fortuitous thing, given the resemblance between the two men). Elordi has been gravitating to literary projects—most obviously Frankenstein (for which he was nominated for every major acting award). Recently, he has also starred in Emerald Fennell’s 2026 adaptation of Emily Bronte’s Wuthering Heights, and the miniseries adaptation of Richard Flanagan’s Booker-prize winning novel The Narrow Road to the Deep North which was released on Prime Video, last year. Recently, he also played Elvis Presley in Sofia Coppola’s Priscilla and co-starred in Ridley Scott’s postapocalyptic thriller The Dog Stars.

This marks Elordi’s first turn as a producer (not executive producer); Scott Stuber of United Artists and Nick Nesbitt will produce, in addition to Elordi’s manager Matt Vioral and Sherry Marsh.

Schiller, whose photographic legacy is entwined with the landmark moments of the 20th century, was the last person to photograph Marilyn Monroe before she died. He also photographed Lee Harvey Oswald the night he was killed, and Jack Ruby moments after he killed Oswald. He photographed Paul Newman and Robert Redford on the set of Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (and also directed the photographic section of the film), and captured the Watts riots and the Electric Kool-Aid Acid Tests. He captured landmark touchdowns by O. J. Simpson and Muhammad Ali defeating Floyd Patterson to win the World Heavyweight Boxing Title. As a filmmaker, he made numerous projects for television, and won an Emmy in 1986 for his adaptation of Peter the Great. He collaborated with O.J. Simpson on a book called I Want to Tell You, while Simpson was in prison, and after he was acquitted, collaborated with former Time magazine journalist Jim Willwerth to write the New York Times bestseller American Tragedy: The Uncensored Story of the Simpson Defense. His photos and stories appeared in countless publications, including Life, Paris Match, The New Yorker, Time, Newsweek, and the Saturday Evening Post.

Olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. Her other work appears in Vanity Fair, Vulture, Lapham's Quarterly, AirMail, the Los Angeles Review of Books, Public Books, The Baffler, Bright Wall/Dark Room, Politics/Letters, The Toast, Truly Adventurous, and elsewhere. She has a PhD from the departments of English/comparative literature and theatre at Columbia University, where she was the Marion E. Ponsford fellow. She hosts the podcasst "Culture Schlock" at Lit Hub Radio. She is on instagram at @oldebean, twitter at @oldrutigliano, and bluesky at @oliviarutigliano.bsky.social.

#7773. Back At The Mayflower

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The first day of the 2026 Federalist Society Convention is in the can. There is much to report.

First, it is good to be back at the Mayflower--well at least good for those of us who made it in. Several years ago, FedSoc decided to move from the Mayflower to the Hilton, a much larger venue. The group had simply outgrown the classic hotel. The downside, of course, is that the Hilton is a terrible hotel. There were assassination attempts on two Presidents at the "Hinkley Hilton." There was no common meeting area, and attendees had to traverse a labyrinth of hallways between sessions. Worse, the rooms were a decade overdue for renovation. We hated it. But most of us were able to fit in.

This year, the registration for the national convention filled up almost instantaneously. I had planned to bring many of my students, but they simply never made it off the waiting list. Longtime members were hanging out in the lobby, hoping to make it off the waiting list, with no luck. I heard that the Harvard FedSoc chapter scheduled a conference for students who could not get in--apparently known as the "shadow docket." People complained to me, as if it was my fault we went back to the small Mayflower because of my carping about the Hilton. I get blamed for everything.

FedSoc will have to figure out what to do for next year, the 40th Anniversary of the National Lawyers Convention. We could always try to check out the new East Wing Ballroom, assuming Judge Leon doesn't enjoin it! The Gaylord Hotel in Maryland could fit everyone, but I am still scarred from the gala dinner there in 2016. I have long been a fan of holding the convention outside of D.C. It would send the exact right message. The times where people in D.C. offices can just stop by for a few panels are long gone. (The sold out registration means only those willing to attend the entire program will be there.) And anyone who wants to speak on the program of this platform should be willing to get on a flight. I would have recommended Texas for the venue, but we will soon be in hostile territory. Perhaps the free state of Florida is the last, best hope.

Second, the format of the FedSoc conference is different. I was so accustomed to the usual rhythm, I feel a bit disoriented. There are no breakout panels. Every panel is a "showcase" panel in the Grand Ballroom. The other rooms are overflow rooms with screens to watch the programming. The schedule is all different. The Rosenkranz Debate was on Thursday afternoon rather than Saturday afternoon over lunch. The Bork and Olson Lectures are both on Friday. And the program ends on Saturday at 2:15, about three hours earlier than usual. Also, instead of having lunchtime panels, all of the rooms on the second floor host smaller, intimate lunches. You could sit at a table with a judge and eight others to chat about an interesting topic. I was at Chief Judge Elrod's table to learn about the Lord of the Rings. (Trigger warning for commenters: I have never read any of those books, I fell asleep during the first movie, and never watched the others.) The discussion was fun! There are some judges who treat their judicial sinecures like Gollum treats the ring. How precious.

I see pros and cons to the new format. On the plus side, this format was far less overwhelming. I routinely felt drained by all of the content. Also, I always felt like I was missing something when I committed to a panel. As a result, I would often bounce between different panels, ensuring that I missed stuff. On the negative side, I enjoyed the ability to pick different panels that may be of interest. I thought the practice groups put on a wide arrange of topical panels. Moreover, there are far fewer speaking slots available with only a few panels each day. These are prime opportunities for up-and-coming members. Still, for this America 250 celebration, I liked the theme in which each panel was framed around a few words from the Declaration. This is an area I have studied for years, and I still learned quite a lot. I don't think we could have kept the Declaration theme going with breakouts.

Third, there is a much stronger focus on students--the lifeblood of Fedsoc. I appreciated that each panel was introduced by a student, rather than the chair of the practice group. During the Scalia dinner, the winners of the Feddie student chapter awards were asked to stand up. I am so proud of the South Texas Chapter, and my students Ryan Lanier and Makayla Arthur, for winning the Hamilton Award for "Most Improved Chapter." Matthew Weinstein, the President of the UCLA chapter during the Percival protest, was given a courage award. And each of the Soc! lunchtime tables was hosted by a student chapter leader.

We can never forget that FedSoc was founded by a bunch of law students. Old people (present company included) need to always give the youth these sorts of opportunities. It wasn't that long ago that I met Will Scharf at the Mayflower, and now he is White House Counsel. I can say the same for so many current judges and other officials that I met when I was student. Indeed, some of the current judges hosted me as a Professor at their chapters! (In 2033, I'll be 49.)  Everything that rises must converge.

Fourth, the decoration of the Mayflower and the Marriott Marquis ballroom was top-notch. There is red, white, and blue bunting all over the Grand Ballroom. The backdrop of the Scalia dinner was expertly done, topped off with George Washington's bible! (No, we couldn't touch it.) The Marine Corp band played during the processional. The Madison Club reception was no longer crammed into a tiny, dark, and noisy tent. It was held in a spacious atrium at the Marquis. Moreover, Madison Club members have access to Edgar's as a lounge to get food and snacks during the day. What a really, really smart idea. This sort of attention to detail matters, at least to me.

Fifth the security is intense. Registration is now available on the lower level. No one is allowed into the hallway without showing credentials and passing through a body scanner. Large bags are banned and smaller bags are searched. The busses from the Mayflower to the Marquis were swept for security, and there was a National Guardsman on board. It is a sad commentary that we have to take these precautions. But with an actual assassination attempt against Justice Kavanaugh, I think we have to accept these costs. (During the Scalia Dinner, Justice Alito praised the courage of Justices Kavanaugh and Barrett for joining the Dobbs decision, knowing what risks that could bring.)

Sixth, I was sort of expecting the vibe at the Mayflower to be grim in light of last week's election. I remember how the 2008 convention felt something like a funeral. I think the mood was mostly one of shock. There are efforts in play to figure out how to deal with the loss of Attorneys General in Texas, Ohio, Iowa, and Kansas. Other states will have to pick up the heavy lifting. Lawyers in Austin can find safe refuge in Baton Rouge, Jackson, St. Louis, Nashville, Tallahassee, Montgomery, and other cities. I am currently researching the laws of intervention on both the plaintiff and defendant side, confessions of error in criminal cases, as well as standing for state legislators and the state senate. The agenda has shifted.

Seventh, one thing I love about the National Convention is that business is conducted right in the hallways. There is a strong sentiment to do everything we can to confirm the remaining judges. These aren't quite the midnight judges of the outgoing Federalist Party, but we are in a similar mindset. There is a universal agreement that Judge Rudofsky was screwed. I second everything my friend Rob Luther wrote in this op-ed in the Arkansas newspaper. And there is a concerted effort to help Elliot Gaiser get across the finish line. What a complete waste if this seat is left for James Talarico to fill. Talk about cutting off your nose to spite your six-gendered face. And then there's Todd Butler. Had the election turned out differently, things may have gone differently. But he is on the path to confirmation. I hope Butler proves me wrong--and he will have a quick opportunity to do so. The January en banc siting has a huge 922(g) case and a challenge to Texas's social media law. As for the new Eighth Circuit nominee, Cody Hiland, he have to prove a lot of people wrong.

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7772. Katie Collom on exploring her relationship with true crime in a suspense novel

My first encounter with the genre was during an annual trip to visit my grandma. Each year, I’d dive into the pile of Reader’s Digest she’d acquired, devouring them cover to cover. It was in one these that I read an article about a criminal profiler who suffered a mental breakdown.

This left a deep impression on my eleven-year-old mind. I couldn’t believe there were human beings who could commit acts so horrific, they actually drove their pursuers insane. More importantly, there were people whose jobs were to figure out how sociopaths think!

I continued to seek out more content about criminals and their crimes. The effect could be…less than healthy. I recall spending a night at a friend’s house and being unable to sleep because it was located somewhat near a railroad track. Just the week before, I’d watched a show about a killer who chose his victims by their proximity to the trains he freight-hopped.

Later as a teenager, my worries became more specific: I’d fret daily about my parents properly locking the windows and doors in our home before we all went to bed. Thankfully we didn’t have a basement or an attic because if we did, I probably wouldn’t have ever gotten a solid night’s sleep.

It wasn’t until I was an adult that these types of articles and shows were given a label. By then, true-crime podcasts and TV series had become so trendy they were their own genre. The sudden abundance of content seemed tailor-made for someone like me: a person who’d been consuming these stories steadily from childhood. Even better, there was a whole community out there, who shared similar obsessions.

(If you’re here, reading this essay, it’s fair to say you know exactly what I mean. You’re one of my people!)

In my new thriller, The Terrarium, my main character is a true-crime obsessed cat sitter named Annie. The isolating nature of her job—going into people’s homes to care for their cats—lends itself to a lot of introspection. For Annie, it manifests in her fanaticism for a podcast called Cuppa Crime.

Her relationship with Cuppa Crime is an emotional crutch. Its hosts, Gail and Gary, Annie’s voices of reason. Whenever she’s anxious, afraid, or bored, she escapes into the tales of heinous crimes that Gail and Gary spin on their podcast. I was interested in seeing how far I could push Annie’s obsession. In turn, this made me stop and study my own relationship with true crime.

Like Annie, I’m a bit of a cliché: a millennial woman who probably consumes just a little too much true crime. It’s no secret that the audience leans very heavily toward women. Additionally, the victims in most popular stories—whether that be books, podcasts, or TV series—also tend to be disproportionately women.

In some ways, this makes it easy to explain away any discomfort I might feel around the genre. I rationalize that I consume it to learn how to protect myself as a woman. Or because I can empathize deeply with the female victims. Or because I want to gain an understanding of how evil people think.

In The Terrarium, Annie drip-feeds herself a constant stream of true crime. Her fascination with it veers into paranoia, and yet, she doesn’t see a problem with it because her overconsumption is for the ‘right’ reasons. Annie’s goal is to unravel the mysteries featured in the Cuppa Crime episodes she listens to. She wants justice and therefore struggles to see when it’s all too much.

Granted, a lot of Annie’s choices are downright chaotic and not things I’d ever do. But I also know how easy it is to cross the line between a healthy amount of true crime and consuming so much that it starts to have a very real effect on your life.

While all my reasons for engaging with the genre ring true, there is a point where too much knowledge becomes a jumble of information with few tangible benefits. Will listening to yet another podcast episode or watching another documentary really teach me how to better protect myself, to empathize, to understand the way the mind of a psychopath works (spoiler: you can’t and never will)?

Since these books, podcasts, and shows are presented as entertainment, it can be easy to consume it the same way you might binge Love is Blind. When the subject matter is so dark, too much too fast can be dicey.

I’m not planning to give up true crime any time soon—like I said, we go way back. But I’m learning to find a balance between prioritizing my mental health and still enjoying a hobby I’ve had since I was a kid.

Real mysteries continue to fascinate me (I am a thriller writer after all) and there’s nothing quite like sinking your teeth into a well-done series. And…if it’s okay to wear shirts with a stranger’s name on them and get way too invested in a bunch of guys throwing a ball around, I think spending your time engaging with true crime is equally valid.

It just doesn’t hurt to be a little more intentional. To pause and consider my reasons for listening to, watching, or reading something in the genre and the impact it can have on me. I remind myself that it’s okay to take a break! These stories will still be there when I’m ready to come back to them.

In some ways, I see myself in the paranoid cat-sitter I’ve created, and I hope you will too. Annie was a fun character to write and, hopefully, a fun character to read in a sort of peek-through-your-fingers way. She certainly has some entertaining ways of coping with her love for true crime, but that’s what makes her so compelling.

Like Annie does with Cuppa Crime, you might just get more than you bargained for when you step into The Terrarium. But don’t worry, you’ll be fine. Just keep your wits about you and (as Gail and Gary like to say) always trust your gut.

Katie Collom is the author of Peter Miles Has to Die. She grew up in Mazatlan, Mexico, and is a life-long expat and world traveler. She spent four years in Texas and has carried a piece of it with her ever since. Currently, she resides in York, England, with her husband and three cats.

#7771. 2 BigLaw firms face proposed class actions over cyber breaches

In newly filed proposed class action lawsuits, plaintiffs are alleging that cyberattacks at Baker McKenzie and Squire Patton Boggs led to exposure of their personal information. (Image from Shutterstock)

In newly filed proposed class action lawsuits, plaintiffs are alleging that cyberattacks at Baker McKenzie and Squire Patton Boggs led to exposure of their personal information.

The complaint against Baker McKenzie was filed in the Northern District of Illinois on Wednesday. According to Reuters, Baker McKenzie said last week a cybercriminal in August “socially engineered two of our users” to obtain a limited number of files, but that “there was no independent malicious access to our system.”

Squire Patton Boggs disclosed its breach in October, saying it involved “an unauthorized third party obtaining a limited set of information from the firm,” Reuters reports.

The complaint against Squire Patton Boggs was also filed Wednesday but in the Northern District of Ohio.

Neither law firm responded to requests for comment from Reuters.

#7770. Deep cuts: The vampire stories that inspired Caitlin Starling’s new novel, ‘Milkteeth’

You’ve watched or read (or both!) Interview with the Vampire, Dracula, Sinners, and all the other heavy-hitters, you’ve dabbled in playing Vampire: The Masquerade…now what?

You could always check out Milkteeth, my newest novel, which asks the burning question: what if vampires had to breastfeed?

…I promise it makes more sense in context.

More seriously, it’s about Beatrice, a vampiric broodmother; she raises the fledgling children of other vampires through the first three years of their transformation, until they are both mentally mature and able to consume human blood safely. Beatrice is very good at what she does, but she’s looked down on with a certain amount of disgust by the vampires who rely on her.

When she takes on a challenging new charge and her body begins to change in inexplicable ways, she has to figure out a solution before everything can be taken for her—or worse, she devours her own brood.

It’s equal parts domestic and rancid, filthy and tender, violent and intimate. And if that’s less your speed, or you want to see some of the works that are responsible, at least in part, for Milkteeth’s existence, here are some lesser-known vampire stories that I’ve enjoyed.

If you’ve heard of anything on this list, I’d wager it’s this show. Running three seasons on Showtime, Penny Dreadful brought together a broad variety of Victorian pulp horror into an atmospheric, brutal, and occasionally messy symphony. While there are a lot of moving parts, Eva Green’s character, Vanessa Ives, finds herself embroiled on a take on Dracula that is lushly horrific.

The combination of corrupted filth and glittering set pieces across the span of the series epitomizes one of my favorite things about vampire stories: how the seduction and the rot are one and the same, and are inextricably linked.

Buehlman’s novel, set in the 1970s Manhattan subway system, is horrifically, wonderfully rancid, with an all-consuming voice and style. His vampires are monsters in every sense of the word, and their charisma comes from their monstrosity, not in spite of it. He also poses a question that I loved, and kept in mind when writing Milkteeth: what would scare a vampire?

Tom Hiddleston and Tilda Swinton star as Adam and Eve, two vampires who have loved each other for centuries, but often spend long periods apart. When Adam descends into a deep depression, Eve comes home to visit.

The movie is a meditation on music, art, and, ultimately, faith in the coming and going of cycles, and the ability of even the unchanging undead to reinvent themselves on occasion. It’s also occasionally hilarious. Seeing this in a little independent theater with a glass of red wine indelibly shaped the writer I grew into.

Speaking of formative vampires, I saw Hellsing for the first time shortly after it was translated into English. It’s on the dark and brutal side of vampire stories, filled with vicious killers, relentless cravings for blood, and a large helping of ominous and cruel bureaucracy. Alucard, bound to serve the descendants of Abraham Van Helsing, seeks out and destroys other undead monsters, but he’s hardly tame. It’s a great reminder that vampires hunt; it’s definitional.

Hellsing has more than a few adaptations, including Hellsing Ultimate, which stays closer to the original manga source. I think I owe myself a rewatch!

If you prefer your vampires more on the domestic side, Dead Collections is a brilliant, funny, and intimate take on the genre. Sol, an archivist who also happens to be a vampire, and so rarely leaves his place of work, falls in love with the widow of a television writer come to donate the papers of her late wife, and in the process begins to grapple with what his vampirism really means. Like the archive he works in, he’s now immortal…but always at risk of arbitrary destruction.

And while vampire stories often deal with legacy and the hidden costs of immortality, Dead Collections does it all from a delightfully fresh (and queer) angle. In particular, its focus on coming to terms with a changed body echo through Milkteeth.

I read Woman, Eating while editing Milkteeth. The two are quite different, with Woman, Eating centering on a young vampire trying to engage in the larger mortal world, and her experiences with art and isolation, but they both return again and again to that most central vampiric curse: the endless hunger.

Try Woman, Eating if you’re in the mood for something on the literary side that will still manage to unsettle you.

There’s a wide world of vampire-inspired stories out there. If any of these stories capture you, follow where they lead. You may discover a whole new way to look at our favorite thirsty monstrous mirrors.

Caitlin Starling writes horror-tinged speculative fiction of all flavors. Her first novel, The Luminous Dead, won the LOHF Best Debut Award and was nominated for both the Bram Stoker and Locus Awards. She is also the author of the gothic horror tales Yellow Jessamine and The Death of Jane Lawrence, as well as a novella in the Vampire: The Masquerade audio collection, Walk Among Us. Her nonfiction has appeared in Nightmare and Uncanny. Starling also works in narrative design, and has been paid to invent body parts. She's always on the lookout for new ways to inflict insomnia.

#7768. Snowbound suspense: 5 thrillers set during snowstorms

A glorious snowfall can conjure up warm thoughts of hot cocoa, kids tossing snowballs and building forts, the holidays, a still, peaceful white landscape. But it can also create a darker, dangerous flipside. Getting trapped, losing power, being exposed to the elements. I’ve always loved thrillers that take advantage of a bad snowstorm–of bringing cold, heartless motivations to frozen landscapes.

In my latest novel, The Cold Read, I take full advantage of the chilling nature of a snowy locale by setting my book at a remote, abandoned ski resort, where the elements quickly take on a very sinister nature.

Here are a few other books that do the same. If you want to shiver your way through a good mystery without actually having to worry about frostbite, you’ll want to pick up these other snowbound stories as we head into the winter season.

This novel, involving a group of co-workers setting off on a retreat, would be a nightmare on its own even without the thriller elements. Traveling with coworkers! Skits! Presentations! The terror! To make things much, much worse, however, this work retreat involves an avalanche, power loss, and the little matter of the group disappearing and dying off.

The characters make this book the tense, twisty thriller it is. It’s an enjoyable puzzle to piece together as you read.

A group of competitive snowboarding friends reunite in the French alps at the ski resort where their frenemy mysteriously disappeared some years before. But weird things immediately start to happen. Their cell phones disappear and they are cut off from the rest of the world when the  cable cars stop working, leaving them stranded on a dangerous mountain. Tensions abound as past secrets and suspicions start to emerge.

Told in dual timelines, the book does a great job of showing how fierce friendships can be both invigorating and toxic.

Martin Edwards, Miss Winter in the Library With a Knife

Six writers and editors are invited to an exclusive Christmas retreat to play a murder mystery game. The setting is remote, the weather is bad, and the guests all have had recent terrible luck in their careers and relationships.

In a classic Golden Age style with an homage to Clue, the novel sets the reader as another player in the game, complete with a “clue finder” guide and puzzles to solve. When the game becomes reality and people start getting bumped off, all bets are off and the competitive guests have to start playing as though their lives depended on it–because they do.

When a woman and her son arrive on a bus during a snowstorm in New York, escaping an abusive situation, service worker Mattie breaks the rules of her job and brings them to her own house instead of the local shelter. This mistake proves costly as the storm intensifies, an intruder begins to stalk them, and strange things begin happening.

Tightly plotted and claustrophobic, I had a tough time reading this one late into the evening.

The Winter Over follows a small group of Antarctic research scientists setting up for the winter over at Shackleton South Pole Research Facility in Antarctica. They are supposed to be tested physically and psychologically to prepare for the conditions and the loneliness–nine weeks of complete isolation, constant darkness, and extreme cold.

As Cass, a newbie to the job, starts to settle in to her work, a suspicious death of one of the crew makes her wonder if someone on the team might’ve snapped. Trapped at base with a killer and nowhere to go, the team doesn’t know who to trust. What will kill them first? The extreme conditions or the humans on base?

Tara Laskowski is the award-winning author of the suspense novels The Cold Read, The Weekend Retreat, The Mother Next Door, and One Night Gone. She also wrote two short story collections, Modern Manners for Your Inner Demons and Bystanders. She has won the Agatha Award and Thriller Award for her short fiction and was the longtime editor of the online flash fiction journal SmokeLong Quarterly. She lives in Virginia with her husband, crime writer Art Taylor, and their son Dashiell.

#7767. Russell Brand found guilty of rape, sexual assault as judge promises ‘sentence of some length’

British comedian, actor and podcaster Russell Brand arrives at the Southwark Crown Court in London on the fourth day of his trial on charges of rape, sexual assault and indecent assault. Brand pleaded not guilty to all charges. (Photo from Shutterstock)

Actor and comedian Russell Brand was found guilty in London on Thursday of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.

The four-week trial, which happened in the Southwark Crown Court in London, examined seven charges brought by six women from 1999 to 2009.

Brand, 51, initially faced three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. He was convicted of four encounters, including a 2004 sexual assault involving grabbing a woman’s breasts in London’s Soho district and the rape of another woman inside his home in 2009.

High Court of England and Wales Judge Joel Bennathan rejected Brand’s bail application, remanded him to custody and told him to expect “a custodial sentence of some length,” according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

Brand is expected to be sentenced Monday. He denied the charges during his four-hour testimony, saying the sexual encounters were consensual. He is also being investigated for additional rape allegations made by two other women.

#7765. The Giggler: The forgotten serial killer who haunted Boston’s South Station

Boston’s South Station was less than 70 years old in 1969 but seemed much older. It certainly lacked the glamour of nearby North Station, home to the Boston Garden, where the city’s basketball and hockey teams played and where the Rolling Stones and James Brown performed for screaming teenagers. In comparison, the South Station stop on 700 Atlantic Avenue was a dreary place for tired daily commuters on their way to the suburbs of the South Shore. With its high-domed ceiling and rickety escalators built during the Depression era, South Station managed to be both enormous and decrepit, a sickly old giant in need of urgent care. As the Boston Globe said a few years later, the once thriving railroad stop was “now staggering along in the last stages of neglect.”

Yet even as it faced the threat of the wrecking ball, the station remained busy, particularly at holiday time. On Friday, December 26, a 9-year-old Dorchester boy named Kenny Martin wandered into the station with a friend, Thomas Lydon. It was the day after Christmas and Kenny, who had come into Downtown Boston to buy some Boy Scout equipment, spent the afternoon horsing around with Lydon at the station. They’d chased each other up and down the escalators, running through the crowd of postholiday shoppers. As the afternoon came to an end, Lydon departed, while Kenny planned to take the train back home.

In his brown-checked jacket with fur collar, blue bell-bottom pants, and orange work boots, Kenny was a typical Dorchester boy, coming home from a day of fun. He was the youngest of four children, small for his age at less than 50 pounds. It might seem odd for a boy so young to be alone in the city, but Boston kids learned to use the subways early in those days. They often traveled on their own from one side of the city to the other.

The platform where he would’ve waited for the Dorchester train was cold and drafty, for there are few places colder than a Boston subway platform in late December. One could only stand and shiver, waiting for the sound of a faraway bell to warn people of approaching trains. Perhaps Kenny looked down the long, dark tunnel for the sign of a subway car’s light, usually visible long before the car was in the station. The tunnels were foreboding; there were stories of people accidentally getting electrocuted on the infamous “third rail” and of huge rodents living in the underground network. Meanwhile, pigeons, bats, and owls roosted in the rafters, occasionally swooping down to frighten the commuters.

There was no shortage of urban legends around South Station, of how people committed suicide by jumping in front of moving trains and how homeless men wandered in the dark tunnels to sleep underneath cardboard coverings. In time, stories of vagrants evolved into stories of trolls living in the tunnels, trolls who only came out after midnight when the station was closed. This was fantasy stuff, tales told by older kids to tease younger ones.

Of course, the station had its good points. It was a historical landmark, after all, opening for business in 1899 as the largest station in the country, a majestic building made of pink granite. There was also the railroad chapel, Our Lady of the Railways. Built in the 1950s, it was the first of its kind in America. Organ music played during every Sunday service, and Boston’s Archbishop Cushing held special masses and Easter vigils, perfect for travelers who couldn’t get home in time to worship. There was a lunch counter, a newsstand, the Sidecar Bar-Grill, a bakery, and a barbershop. A Paramount film crew had been to South Station earlier in the year to shoot a scene for a Jack Lemmon movie, The Out of Towners. For a few days, the dilapidated old station was enlivened by the buzz of Hollywood energy and curious crowds. Despite these occasional bright spots, the atmosphere remained glum and ramshackle. When the crowds thinned out after the rush hour, all that remained were boarded-up areas that always seemed to be “under construction” and weary cleaning crews wiping out the messes of the day.

At some point in the afternoon of December 26, Kenny met a pudgy, dark-haired man with a round face. The man seemed different from the other people hurrying around the station. He was rumpled. He needed a shave and a bath. It turned out the man was also named Kenneth. What they talked about, or how they spent their next few hours together, is unknown. History would reveal that the unshaven man knew all about the secret tunnels in South Station and knew all the special places where people could hide. He may have offered to show Kenny around the old building, an irresistible prospect for a 9-year-old boy.

Kenny’s body was found eleven days later. He’d been strangled to death. His body was hidden in one of the station’s underground passageways. Someone had wrapped it in a canvas bag and covered it with debris. A search team consisting of police from two districts, as well as city engineers, had spent the day exploring sewers and tunnels around the station. The search ended in an abandoned transit tunnel, a ghostly location that had once been used to transport cargo to the surface cars. It was a dingy place for a little boy to wind up, cold and dark and airless.

He could’ve been lured there only by one of the station’s trolls.

Security guards patrolled South Station and routinely tossed out vagrants and drunks, shoving them out the door onto Atlantic Avenue. These scenes were unpleasant, but the guards were under orders to keep the winos and grifters out. The raggedy station only looked worse if pitiful old drunks were lounging on the wooden benches. Yet Kenneth Harrison, the pudgy man, had been living in the place for nearly a year, like a hermit hiding in a cave. He didn’t have to compete for a bed at one of the nearby shelters, not when he could hunker down in one of the abandoned offices beneath the station.

The morning after he’d killed Kenny Martin, Harrison slouched out into the daylight, searching for a rooming house where he could find a bed and lie low. The sidewalk was still slippery from the previous night’s rain and sleet. It would have been a nice day to hang out at the station, yet Harrison felt it was time to go. Hanging around was too risky, even if the dead boy was buried deeper than an old bone.

Harrison had grown up in Roxbury’s Mission Hill neighborhood and had dropped out of school after the eighth grade. Now, at 31, he was an unemployed restaurant worker, living a vagabond’s existence and spending what little money he had on alcohol. He’d become one of life’s losers, a degenerate barfly with no future. He was virtually indistinguishable from dozens of others in his situation. The difference was that Harrison murdered children.

Kenny Martin, whose face would soon be featured in local newspapers, was Harrison’s second young victim. Two-and-a-half years earlier, Harrison had killed a 6-year-old girl named Lucy Palmarin. She’d been cashing in an empty tonic bottle at a store. Witnesses saw her climbing into the car of an unknown man. She was found floating among the garbage in South Boston’s Fort Point Channel, a mile from her home. Since the medical examiner found no signs of injury or foul play, Lucy’s death was ruled an accidental drowning. Lucy’s disappearance created a flurry of activity in South Boston. Posters with her picture were distributed throughout the community. Her poor mother waited up nights, clutching a book of old photographs of the missing girl. Three weeks into the search, the Boston police called in the FBI for assistance. They suspected a kidnapping, but the truth was worse.

On April 15, 1967, Harrison was driving a cab, among his many odd jobs. He would later tell a judge that he had dropped off a fare near the D Street housing project where Lucy lived. He saw her walking and offered to give her a ride. Instead of taking her home, he drove to the channel where he tossed her in the city’s notoriously dirty water.

In another version of the confession, Harrison said the little girl asked him for a quarter, which led to him giving her a piggyback ride. Once she was up on his back, he easily pitched her into the water. So he said. His confessions sounded ludicrous. Lucy’s family was Puerto Rican and new to America. The girl didn’t speak English. In between the two child murders, Harrison had killed two adults. There’d been a barroom beef with a fellow named Joseph Breen, an ex-marine and water company employee. Harrison and Breen had been drinking at the Novelty Bar in Boston’s Combat Zone, a dank neighborhood of nudie bars and X-rated theaters.

Later, after an argument over money, Harrison beat Breen to death with a rock.

Inexplicably, Harrison called the police that night, telling them they could find Breen’s body floating in an excavation pit on Kneeland Street near Chinatown. When the police asked who was calling, Harrison felt a laugh coming up his throat, like an eruption.

It was a time when killers were becoming celebrities, with memorable names and trademarks, like the Boston Strangler or the Zodiac in California. Why couldn’t Harrison be “The Giggler?”

Harrison must’ve felt as elusive as the Zodiac, because he’d actually returned to the Novelty a short time later. A couple of Breen’s friends were there and recognized him as the man who had been with Breen the night he was killed. Breen’s friends called the police, but by the time they arrived, Harrison was gone again, no doubt back at the train station, hiding in plain sight.

Then, just a month before killing Kenny Martin, Harrison had murdered an old woman, 75-year-old Clovis Parker of South Boston. As he’d done with the little girl, he left Clovis floating in Fort Point Channel, a mere five-minute walk from Harrison’s South Station hideout. He’d tell investigators that he had met the old woman on a bridge, and she’d asked for help getting across. Without giving a reason, Harrison said that he’d simply kicked Clovis Parker’s cane from under her and then tossed her over the guardrail. The unfortunate woman’s death hadn’t even made it to the newspapers.

A few days after killing Kenny Martin, Harrison called his sister, Eileen. He confessed that he had killed a boy and told her where the body was hidden. On January 6, the day Kenny’s body was found, Harrison boarded a train at South Station and left Boston.

Eileen consulted a lawyer and then called the police. They followed her tip to find the body, and then a quartet of detectives armed with an arrest warrant traced Harrison to Providence. They arrested him without incident and held him without bail in Suffolk County.

While detectives questioned him about Kenny Martin’s death, Harrison interrupted.

“As long as I’m here,” he said, “I might as well tell you about a few more.”

He told them about Lucy Palmarin, Joseph Breen, and Clovis Parker. Investigators were stunned. Harrison was confessing to four murders committed over a span of thirty-two months.

When he talked about Kenny Martin, Harrison said he’d had “an urge to kill” but didn’t remember doing anything. He merely woke up the next morning and saw the boy with a rope around his neck.

Harrison showed little emotion as he spoke, but he seemed comfortable talking about his crimes. He even took a liking to the detectives interrogating him. Later, when he learned that one of the detectives had retired, Harrison sent a card.

Yet his frankness about the murders and his friendship with the detectives masked a fragile mind.

#7764. Chimera

Rina Varger beat her palm against the old Ford pickup’s door in time to Aerosmith’s “Push Comes to Shove” as she drove across the bridge and into town. It was the morning of the tenth of September and the Merrimack was running high after a week of torrential rain, debris and dead brush from upriver borne along by the surging brown water. The wind in her face felt good after a day spent scrubbing years of dust and nameless gunk from between sticky floorboards. Everything had to be perfect for Aunt Eleanor’s wedding. Nana Marian was losing her mind trying to get the house in shape, running their skinless maid Kate Bartlett ragged.

A little after eight Rina parked in front of Julian and Eddie’s place, a cramped two-story bungalow with a patchy lawn and huge stands of sumac nearly obscuring its front entrance and encroaching on its drive-way. Julian, an aging queen cast off by a prominent Cape Cod family, owned Plover Antiques downtown. Eddie Means was a veterinarian at the Franklin Park Zoo in Boston, and had been the Varger family’s meat man for almost ten years. Rina killed the engine and stepped out onto the curb, fishing in her jacket pockets for her cigarettes. She was about to light up when she heard voices coming from the direction of the driveway. She pocketed her smokes and went around the house, moving slowly, keeping to the shadows of the sumac stand.

Four teenage boys, maybe fifteen or sixteen, and a girl who looked a little younger stood in a half circle at the end of the driveway, in front of Julian’s garage. Another girl, maybe a year or two older than the others, sat fenced in by their little gang with her back against the peeling garage door. Even from the curb, Rina could see the shiner discoloring her left eye and cheekbone. As she watched, one of the boys kicked the seated girl in the ribs. She gasped, bending double.

“Show us,” the biggest boy demanded. He was the whole pack-age, letter jacket and crew cut, neck and shoulders like a bull. “Come on, freak. Let’s see if it’s true.”

Rina bent and scooped up a stone from the lawn’s sandy edge, stepping out into the center of the driveway. She weighed the rock in her palm, sizing up the distance between her and the gang. Her mother would have stomped right into the middle of them, screaming that she’d call their parents. Her grandfather would have thrown his skin off then and there and gone for their throats. Her grandmother would have watched. “Somewhere down the middle,” Rina muttered to herself.

“I’ll do it myself,” said the boy. He knelt, a look of strange, compulsive hunger making him seem older than his years. The girl squeezed her eyes shut tight and pressed herself against the garage door. Rina took a deep breath, did her best Bruce Hurst windup, and threw the rock as hard as she could. The boy turned at her grunt of effort and took it square in the nose, his head snapping back like a speed bag. He went down on his ass with a shriek, clapping his hands over his gushing nose. Blood dripped into his lap as the others turned in shock. One went for a pocketknife.

Rina pulled her jacket back to show the revolver stuffed into the waist of her jeans. “Get lost,” she said. The gang stopped cold. She snapped her fingers. “Come on. Time’s a-wastin’.”

They remained frozen for a moment. One of the boys looked at their ringleader, then looked away, shamefaced and red. The girl in their little gang seemed on the verge of tears. Slowly, two of them helped the bleeding boy to his feet and led him past her toward the street. He glared at her in passing, poisonous hate and terror at war behind his beady blue eyes. “Fucking dyke,” he muttered.

“If I see you around here again, you’ll wish I hadn’t,” said Rina. “You got that, tiger?”

He ducked his head and ran, and the others ran after him, the girl looking back fearfully over her shoulder. When she was sure they were gone, Rina went to the girl sitting against the garage door and offered her a hand. She took it. “Thanks.” The girl got unsteadily to her feet, wiping dirt from her shirtfront. She was taller than Rina, chubby and a little stooped, with a round face and buck teeth. When she spoke, it was with the slightest lisp. “I’m Wendy.”

“Julian’s my uncle,” said Wendy, sniffing. “I’m staying with him for a little while.”

Wendy shook her head. “No. He’s okay.” She picked at the cuff of her sweatshirt. “I had, um, some problems with my mom. It’s why I’m out here.”

The side door banged open. Eddie hurried down the concrete steps, shirtless and barefoot in nothing but a pair of tan slacks. He wore a big buck knife on his hip. “You alright, honey?” he asked Wendy, though he didn’t for a moment look away from Rina. Rina smiled, showing all her teeth.

“That’s alright, then. Why don’t you go help your uncle with dinner?”

“Go on in, honey,” he said, firmly this time. Wendy took a hesitant step back, her cheeks reddening, and then fled inside.

“You stay away from that girl, Rina,” said Eddie. “She’s got enough problems.”

Eddie stuck his thumbs in his belt. He was only a few inches taller than Rina, and maybe thirty pounds heavier, but faggot or not, he wasn’t someone you wanted to fight. “Yes.”

Rina shrugged. She hadn’t really thought about Wendy like that, until Eddie told her not to. She tried on the idea of slipping her hands under that baggy sweatshirt, of tilting that soft, rounded chin up for a kiss, sweaty black hair tangled around her fingers. The things you weren’t supposed to eat were always the sweetest. “Fair enough,” she said, clearing her throat. “What you got for me?”

Eddie shook his head and went to lift the garage door. “Broad fucking daylight,” he said as the smell of ripe meat and preservatives billowed out around him in a fragrant cloud. Rina stepped closer, sniffing at the air. In the gloom of the garage, between rusted gym equipment and stacked cardboard boxes, the source of the smell lay wrapped in plastic on a dolly under a frayed blue tarp. Eddie looked back at her. “You may not care who sees you, but I lose my job and you’re gonna have to find someone else to play ball.”

Ignoring him, Rina went to the dolly and knelt, lifting the nearest corner of the tarp. A liquid black eye stared back at her through long, curling lashes. A dead Cape buffalo, maybe a year old, horns not yet fused over the crown of its skull. “Beautiful,” she said. She stood, letting the tarp fall back into place. “I’ll get the ramp.”

The things you weren’t supposed to eat were always the sweetest.

Rina took the back way home, the station crackling through the dead spots on the orchard road so that Captain and Tenille sounded like they were singing from the depths of a bottomless pit. She turned the radio off. She kept thinking of Wendy. Broken birds always got her going. Something about how vulnerable they were, how bad they needed someone to be good to them. Rina liked being that someone, at least at first. If you rode out the crying and the clinginess for a few weeks you could really put your feet up afterward. Coast on goodwill while they made you breakfast and ate you out on the couch.

“You’re just too bad.” She chuckled to herself, lighting a cigarette as she turned onto the old pumping station connector. Weighed down by the buffalo carcass in its bed, the truck thumped and rattled over the broken pavement where it gave way to dirt. The trees—old growth, not pine—crowded close so that their branches formed a tunnel of dappled shade over the road. Part of Rina always felt relief when she turned into that sheltering gloom, like she’d braved the open grasslands on a hunt and come back to the tribe with meat over her shoulder. Sometimes she envied those long-ago Skin Dancers their adventures, the danger they’d faced in a world not yet broken to the saddle.

A flock of wild turkeys darted into the road ahead of Rina. She slowed to let them cross, the tom keeping a wary eye on her as the hens hurried their half-grown pullets along. He was a big one, scarred on his head and neck and missing most of his comb. Not today, thought Rina, smiling at the tom. The fox in her itched and whined, pulling at her thoughts, turning them red and quick. She’d eaten it only a week before, and it still paced restlessly in her mind. You enjoy the weather, old man. We’ll Dance another time.

The big tom gobbled and fluffed his wings. The turkeys disappeared into the woods. Rina drove onward. She passed the burned-out wreck of the Mercer farm, half the big dairy barn still standing thirty-odd years after the fire that had killed three of the Mercers in their beds. Rina’s family owned the land now, but they’d never built on it. The Mercer cows had been sold off for dog food and the forest now crept step by careful step toward the blackened skeletons of the farmhouse and the barn. Rina remembered laying on her back beneath those sagging beams on her sixteenth birthday, bored and frustrated as Fabian La Vigne, her second cousin on Nana Marian’s side of the family, tentatively licked her pussy.

Rina wondered if Eleanor’s marriage would be like that. She’d never pictured Aunt Ellie with a man. Rina had a clear childhood memory of her aunt, maybe nineteen or twenty at the time, splashing in the shallows at Lake Winnisquam with some of their girl cousins from Memé Carlotte’s side of the family up in Maine, the Gerstmanns. Ellie, plump and long-legged in her two-piece, her red hair flying as she skimmed a palm across the surface of the water, droplets sparkling in the air, and that smile, alive with mischief and desire. Now she was marrying Rudy Gerstmann, her third cousin, a tall, soft-spoken man with a sandy mustache and the slender fingers of a pianist. Rina’s great-aunt Simone always said if you married outside the bloodline you’d wind up with chimeric babies, unable to control the Skin Dance. Her late uncle Cecil’s baby with the girl in town he’d fallen for had been stillborn, a patchwork horror of fur and feathers, but her uncle Albert’s bastard, Jean Paul, could Dance as well as any of them, and his mother was a diner waitress. When Rina asked Simone about that, her great-aunt told her it wasn’t decent to talk about matters of the bedroom.

Rina pulled onto Bear Lake Drive, the truck bouncing as it hit dirt road, the trees closing in tight to either side. A half mile in, Alfie Heureaux, one of her grandmother’s men and a distant cousin on the La Vigne side of the family, stood guard at the bottom of the driveway to Hensteeth, leaning against the rusted cattle gate, a lit cigarette dan-gling from his mouth. With his creased, leathery skin and colorless hair he might have been anywhere from fifty to seventy. He had a Dancing scar at the right corner of his mouth that pulled it down a little, and another at his hairline that gave him a little bald triangle above his right temple. He wore a weathered denim jacket over a plaid shirt.

“What’s the word, hummingbird?” he asked as Rina rolled to a stop beside his post, the Ford’s brakes squealing in protest.

“Not a thing, chicken wing,” Rina answered, smiling. “Anyone been down from the house?”

“Camille went out a little while ago.” Alfie blew smoke out his nostrils and inhaled it. He gestured with his cigarette at the tarped mass in the Ford’s bed. “Everything go okay with Siegfried and Roy there?”

“Fine, yeah,” said Rina. “You gonna make me fuckin’ sit here all day listening to you?”

Alfie shadowboxed at her, muttering good-naturedly, then chuckled and went to open the gate. The iron post dragged over the stony ground of the drive. He waved her in. “Someone’s gonna wash that mouth out with soap one of these days, kid,” he called after her.

It was a mile and a half through the woods to Hensteeth, the Varger family compound Rina’s great-grandparents had built at the dawn of the century. Manchester was a rich place then, textile factories booming on both sides of the river, lumber in the hills, distilleries pouring rivers of illegal booze south to Boston and Worcester, north to Concord and the seacoast. Great-grand-père Etienne and Great-grand-mère Antoinette built a mansion that made the governor’s residence at Bridges House look like a garden shed. Rina could see it through the trees, the four-story redbrick facade with its creeping ivy and its mullioned windows, the flash of light on the arboretum glass, and behind them the low bulk of the Old House built back against Thrush Hill, which rose two hundred feet of cut and blasted rock to a wooded ridge where deer sometimes passed by in single file.

Emil sat out in front of the garage in a rusty deck chair, his shotgun propped beside him, when Rina pulled into the circular driveway. He nodded at her. One of the cats, a big black queen, ran out of the bay and between his legs, a mouse in her jaws. She paused to look at Rina for a moment, then darted away into the gardens. Rina put the truck in park and tossed Emil the keys. Gravel crunched beneath her boots. “Make sure this gets to the kitchen,” she told him, jerking her thumb back at the truck’s bed. “Is anyone here yet?”

“Not yet,” he said, shifting his toothpick from one corner of his mouth to the other as he stood. He was tall and very thin, his hair pomaded, his coat fashionable. Emil was Great-aunt Adeline and Great-uncle Louis’s eldest, a distant cousin on the Cotard side of the family, Rina’s great-grand-mère Antoinette’s kin; he’d come down from Quebec just the year before. “They are come later. Ce soir.”

Rina left him to take the Ford around the back of the house. For a while she walked through the gardens, which were thinning out as fall came on, the lilacs long since gone, the pink crab apple blossoms trodden to fragrant, oily humus. She stopped for a while by the piscine, watching the carp swim in the dark green water in the shade of a line of cypress, the morning sky reflected in the surface. She thought about Wendy again. Julian’s niece wasn’t bad-looking. Rina liked a little something to grab on to, even if Wendy was only a kid . . .

Don’t make a problem where there isn’t one, she told herself. She flicked her cigarette butt into the water. A fish swam up to investigate it, then turned and dove. Across the pool, a peacock strutted over mossy stones, its tail feathers dragging in the dust.

On her way to the house, Rina came across her grandmother bedding down the rose bushes, patting mulch over their roots with her long, gnarled hands. Marian Varger was a big woman, two hundred pounds or more, and almost six feet tall. Since Grand-père Henry’s second stroke in ’63 she’d kept the family’s interests in line. The gambling, the loan sharking, the hijacking rings and protection rackets. The first unions in Manchester to try holding back the payments they’d owed her husband had learned the hard way not to cross her. Her Dancing scars must have helped put the fear of God in those hard old New Englanders. Her large, square face looked to have been cut apart and glued together without much regard for symmetry. Her right eye, black and piercing, was a full inch higher than her drooping, milky left, and her nose had been broken several times and flattened slightly on its left side. When she smiled, which wasn’t often, the scars that crisscrossed her lips pulled her face into a grotesque, leering grimace, her gums and teeth showing like a horse’s.

Marian saw Rina and rose, wiping her hands on her apron. They embraced and kissed each other on both cheeks. Marian broke away and held Rina at arm’s length. “Lunch is in an hour,” she said. “Wash up, and change into something decent. You look like a hood.”

“Get,” said Marian, not unkindly, and sent Rina on her way with a swat across the backside. Rina jogged the rest of the way to the house. She was excited for the wedding. Her mother would be a wreck over it, but what else was new? Marguerite had never really been all there. Rina saw other mothers with their kids in town, holding their hands on the street, carrying them in slings and backpacks, rubbing noses and kissing. Playing in the park. All her childhood memories were of her grandmother, or her great-aunt Celene, or Aunt Ellie. She remembered her uncle Harry a little bit from before he’d left. A big smile. Thick black hair. He’d used to give her shoulder rides across the lawn. No one had seen him in twenty years.

Her uncle Albert lay dozing on the landing in the skin of a tiger, watching her with half-closed eyes as she climbed the stairs. The sharp, musky smell of him hung in the air like gasoline fumes.

The house’s foyer was empty, the dark wood of the branching front staircase leading up to the second floor gleaming in the light that came in through the oculus. Kate the maid lurked just to the left of it, dusting a vase with morose intensity. Beyond the landing’s big mullioned windows, the courtyard garden’s old willow swayed in a gentle breeze. Rina took off her boots by the door and crossed the Oriental carpet barefoot, running her palm over the worn brow of the stone lion at the center of the room for luck as she passed by. Her uncle Albert lay dozing on the landing in the skin of a tiger, watching her with half-closed eyes as she climbed the stairs. The sharp, musky smell of him hung in the air like gasoline fumes. His tail, hanging between the handrail’s slats, twitched slowly back and forth.

The third-story hall was silent, but as Rina passed the door to her mother’s room she heard the groan of something heavy moving across the floor. She paused. Kneeling, she looked through the keyhole and into the dimly lit room. Within, Marguerite lay naked on her bed. The curtains were drawn and the late morning sunlight shone through them, weak and reddish. At the foot of the bed, a polar bear stood on its hind legs, towering nearly to the ceiling. Rina watched through the keyhole as the bear approached her mother. She could smell its carrion breath and the oily reek of its yellow-white pelt. It rested one tremendous paw on Marguerite’s leg, its claws dimpling her flesh. It nosed her heavy thighs apart, chuffing softly, and Rina saw a flash of rough pink tongue between her mother’s legs.

“Careful,” Marguerite whispered. “Careful, darling.” Slowly, she wrapped her thighs around the bear’s huge skull. It retreated half a step, dragging her toward the end of her bed, her long auburn hair trailing over the sheets. She let out a squeal of delight and Rina turned away and straightened, her face burning. What did you expect, pervert? She backed up from the door, walking on tiptoe as the sounds from behind it grew quicker and more frenzied. She didn’t know who was with her mother. She didn’t want to.

Rina’s room was the last on the right, its single dormer window looking out over the north lawn and the ridge and the Old House built up flush to the rock face. She flopped down on her narrow twin bed, staring up at her poster of Gene Simmons onstage at the band’s 1977 Madison Square Garden show, his face a grinning death mask, his bare arms slick with sweat. You could tell from the way the tendons in his wrist and on the back of his picking hand stood out that he was really going for it. Balls out. Rina sighed and slipped her hand down the front of her pants. Her skin was hot. Dampness met her fingers.

She’d just jerk off a little, just to come, and to get Wendy out of her head. Blow out the bad vibes from seeing her mother with whoever she was fucking these days. That was all. She closed her eyes, getting to work. Her breath came a little faster.

#7761. Over $157M in pro bono legal services donated by law class of 2026

The class of 2026 has donated more than $157 million in pro bono work, or more than 4.3 million hours in legal services, according to an Association of American Law Schools survey released Friday.

That’s an average of 197 of donated hours per student, according to this fall’s survey of 110 law schools, which reported on 22,249 students, or about 58% of the class of 2026 in ABA-accredited schools. With a value of $36.14 an hour, according to nonprofit coalition Independent Sector, the donated time has an estimated value of $157 million.

And these numbers might be low, according to the report, since the hours are difficult to track and did not include law students in master’s degree programs. Total donated hours could be more than $250 million if average hours per student were applied to the total enrollment of all AALS member law schools, the study states.

In the decade since the survey was established, it has reported more than $1 billion in legal services contributions from law students.

Many law schools now emphasize serving clients in legal deserts. Some offer remote pro bono opportunities and others offer clinics, externships and fellowships. For instance, University of Nebraska College of Law Rural Estate Planning Clinic students provide free estate‑planning services to senior citizens in rural communities, preparing documents like wills, powers of attorney, living wills and transfer‑on‑death deeds.

“Access to justice is a first principle for legal education and the legal profession,” Danielle M. Conway, AALS president, said in the release. “The pro bono and clinical legal work done by today’s law students help to bridge access-to-justice gaps and reinforce the profession’s obligation to serve every community.”

#7757. Legal sector jobs hit record high in October, new data shows

Data from the U.S. Department of Labor shows that employment in the U.S. legal sector hit a record high in October. (Image from Shutterstock)

Legal sector jobs have reached a record high, hitting more than 1.25 million positions for the first time in October, according to seasonally adjusted data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday.

Last month, 1,251,200 people worked in lawyer, paralegal and other law-related professional roles, up 2,400 jobs from September and 3,200 jobs from August, according to Law360, which reported on the government statistics.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics also notes that jobs in the legal sector have increased each month since March, Law360 reports. They have grown by 22,800 year over year.

The broader economy in the United States added 165,000 jobs in October, according to Reuters, which has additional reporting. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1% last month.

According to court documents, Osbeck routinely traveled from the United States to Haiti over the past three decades and sexually abused minors in that country. The charges in the indictment are based on his sexual abuse of a Haitian boy between approximately 2004 and 2008, when the boy was approximately 8 through 12 years old, and his attempt to engage in a commercial sex act around 2019-2020 with another Haitian boy. Osbeck was taken into custody in Haiti at the end of September 2026 after an investigation by Haitian authorities and then returned to the United States on Oct. 14 where he was arrested by U.S. law enforcement upon landing at Miami International Airport. Sheppard, Mullin, Richter & Hampton will require all U.S.-based lawyers and staff to spend four days per week in the office starting in 2027. (Image from Shutterstock)

Sheppard, Mullin, Richter & Hampton has become the latest firm to reverse course on COVID-era hybrid work policies, confirming that in 2027, all U.S.-based lawyers and staff will be required to spend four days per week in the office.

Other notable firms, including Duane Morris and Vinson & Elkins, are also requiring a four-day in-person attendance minimum, according to a report by Law.com.

#7746. Justice Department Announces Actions to Disrupt North Korea’s Massive Theft of Cryptocurrency

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.

“North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement shows that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”

“The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division quickly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.”

“Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”

“By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.”

“The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”

“North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” said Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.”

Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California

Today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California announced the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain.

North Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.

During the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the new victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts.

The North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.

The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.

The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

The Department, FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen From Binance

Separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.

The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and the IRS-CI.

#7745. Defense attorney in Tupac Shakur murder trial discovered dead inside his Vegas home

Attorney Michael Sanft, in court last August during the trial of Duane “Keffe D” Davis, was found dead in his Las Vegas home on Friday. (Daniel Cole/Pool Photo via AP)

The lawyer who defended the man convicted of killing rapper Tupac Shakur was found dead Friday inside his Las Vegas home, a short time after filing an appeal in the case.

Michael Sanft, 55, was the attorney for Duane “Keffe D” Davis, who was found guilty Oct. 13 of first-degree murder in the killing of Shakur. Davis, 63, was sentenced to 40 years to life in prison for being the architect of the drive-by shooting targeting Shakur in 1996 when the rapper was 25 years old, according to the New York Post.

Sanft filed an appeal of the conviction on Oct 30. He had taken Davis’ case pro bono.

Sanft leaves behind two children. The cause of death is pending. Police said Sanft’s death doesn’t appear to be suspicious.
