About the RoleWe're looking for a FinOps Data Engineer to help drive cost optimization and cloud financial governance across our AWS infrastructure and GCP footprint. You'll work cross-functionally with Engineering, Finance, and Product to find and ship savings, build the tooling necessary to maximize efficiency of every dollar spent in the cloud, and cultivate a culture of cost awareness across engineering teams. This role owns the data side of that mission: the models, pipelines, and analysis that make cost, usage, and margin numbers trustworthy across the company.This is a hands-on engineering role, not an analyst seat. You'll do the schlep work other teams don't have time for, digging into a bucket's access pattern, writing the dbt model or Python pipeline that ships the fix, building the cost-vs-revenue mart that answers a margin question once instead of every time, and chasing a number until it reconciles. Strong communication matters as much as technical depth, you'll regularly explain a savings case or a data model's implications to an engineering team, a finance stakeholder, and a leadership audience in the same week.What You'll Be Responsible ForIn this role, you'll:

Find and ship savings across AWS and GCP: Analyze billing, usage, and cost trends to identify opportunities, rightsizing, storage lifecycle policies, data transfer, and spot/auto-scaling. Take ideas from identification through to a realized dollar figure, not just a recommendation.

Build and maintain the FinOps data pipeline: Design and run the BigQuery/dbt models that turn raw billing and usage data (CUR, Storage Lens) into reconciled, trustworthy mart tables, the foundation everything else in FinOps is built on.

Build cost-vs-revenue and customer segmentation models: Model unit economics and margin by product line and customer segment, and extend coverage as new products and segments come online.

Apply data science to cost and usage data: Build forecasting models, detect anomalies statistically rather than by threshold alone, and quantify savings opportunities (e.g. storage lifecycle, request-cost patterns) with rigor a spreadsheet can't match.

Build and maintain cost attribution: Tagging policies, cost allocation, and chargeback/showback so engineering teams can see and own their own spend. This is foundational work other savings work depends on.

Automate cost governance: Build automated cost reporting, anomaly detection, and alerting. Write the scripts and infrastructure-as-code (Python, Terraform, Lambda) that enforce cost policy rather than relying on manual review.

Partner with engineering on architecture decisions: Bring cost into the room early, cost-efficiencies are cheaper to get right at design than to retrofit.

Work with Finance on forecasting and reporting: Support budget tracking and financial KPIs; build dashboards and self-serve analytics engineering and finance can both read.

Have strong AWS expertise and working GCP knowledge, including pricing models, billing structures, and cost optimization mechanics.

Have data engineering depth: dbt, BigQuery (or an equivalent modern warehouse), SQL at scale, and data modeling for analytics (dimensional modeling, incremental models, testing).

Have data science fundamentals: statistical forecasting, anomaly detection, and experimentation, and know when a rigorous model beats a rule of thumb.

Have automation and scripting skills: Python, Terraform/ pulumi, Lambda, or Bash.

Are comfortable with cost/billing tooling: AWS Cost Explorer, Cost & Usage Reports, GCP Billing Reports, and BI/dashboarding (we use Hex).

Have experience with, or are comfortable picking up, Linear and Notion as the system of record for tracking and documenting FinOps work.

Experience with a dedicated cloud cost management platform (e.g. CloudZero, Vantage, or similar) is a plus, not required.

Can analyze cost data and present it clearly to both technical and non-technical audiences.

Have prior experience spanning data analytics, data engineering, or data science in a FinOps, cloud cost management, or cloud governance context.

Are energized by doing the unglamorous, high-leverage work (the schlep) that unblocks other teams, and by working cross-functionally without positional authority.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

#7741. Three men charged in $130M AI impersonation scheme

Three foreign nationals are accused of using artificial intelligence to pose as corporate executives and lawyers in a fraud scheme that allegedly took in over $129 million. (Image from Shutterstock)

Federal prosecutors in Manhattan have unsealed an indictment accusing three foreign nationals of using artificial intelligence to pose as corporate executives and lawyers in a fraud scheme that allegedly took in over $129 million, according a story published Friday in The Guardian.

According to the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan and Guy Sheetrit manipulated voices and images to deceive employees at companies around the world between 2024 and 2026. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain this summer, and Sheetrit was taken into custody in the United Kingdom in September.

According to prosecutors, the scheme worked in two stages. First, the defendants allegedly posed as a company executive and told employees they needed help with a confidential financial matter. Employees were then directed to contact attorneys at a major international law firm, whom the defendants also allegedly impersonated, and to wire large sums as instructed.

Prosecutors allege that the defendants stole nearly $5 million from a Missouri hospital system, about $2.7 million from a Rhode Island bank, roughly $3 million from a California hospital system, more than $4.6 million from a Massachusetts mutual fund, about $5 million from a Florida pet food company, and over $11 million from a U.K. technology company. The defendants have been indicted on charges relating to wire fraud, money laundering, conspiracy and identity theft.

Funds were allegedly routed to accounts in countries including the U.S., Spain, Portugal, Greece, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Austria, Slovakia and China, then converted to cryptocurrency to hide their origin and split among conspirators. Prosecutors say Soall and Hazan used several aliases, including “Rocky Balboa,” “Superman Cash” and “Ron.”

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a statement that while AI holds great promise, it can also be turned to criminal ends.

#7738. Justice Department Announces Actions to Disrupt North Korea’s Massive Theft of Cryptocurrency

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.

“North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement shows that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”

“The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division quickly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.”

“Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”

“By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.”

“The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”

“North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” said Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.”

Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California

Today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California announced the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain.

North Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.

During the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the new victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts.

The North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.

The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.

The effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

The Department, FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen From Binance

Separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.

The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and the IRS-CI.

#7727. Wells Fargo faces labor board complaint over union vote

The National Labor Relations Board alleged the lender threatened and retaliated against workers in favor of unionization at a California branch.

The National Labor Relations Board has accused Wells Fargo of illegally threatening and retaliating against employees and coercing workers to prevent fair unionization votes at a California branch.

Most employees of an Atwater, California, branch who signed cards supporting unionization in December 2023 voted against unionization the following month, a regional director of the NLRB alleged, in a complaint filed Feb. 11 and seen by Bloomberg,

The NLRB claims Wells Fargo coerced workers to vote against unionization. Wells Fargo has denied that allegation.

The labor board wants the bank to recognize and negotiate with the union despite the vote, based on a 2023 precedent case. The 2023 Cemex ruling strengthened the NLRB's power to compel companies that violate labor laws to recognize unions.

However, Republicans and business groups oppose the precedent. The acting general counsel of NLRB, William Cowen, or his permanent replacement, could withdraw, amend, or settle the Wells Fargo complaint.

President Donald Trump appointed Cowen acting general counsel this month, days after firing NLRB’s previous chief lawyer Jennifer Abruzzo, a Biden appointee, and Democratic board member Gwynne Wilcox.

The email notifying Wilcox of her termination said she was being fired since she did not “share the objectives” of the present administration. Wilcox’s ouster has left the board with only two members coupled with existing vacancies and does not meet the minimum number of members needed to adjudicate routine cases.

Wilcox is suing Trump, alleging the president surpassed his authority in firing her and requesting that she be allowed to resume her work as an NLRB member.

The NLRB complaint does not signify a complete investigation or a full adjudication of the allegations; rather, the regional office found that the allegations may be sufficient to go to a hearing to consider all evidence and make credibility determinations, a Wells Fargo spokesperson noted.

Employees at the Atwater branch voted 3-1 to reject unionization in January 2024. The branch manager allegedly told staff she knew about organizing discussions and warned about camera surveillance. She also reportedly told workers that Wells Fargo would apply stricter work conditions and would make union supporters stay longer hours.

A Wells Fargo spokesperson said the bank trains its managers to respect the rights of its employees to freely associate and join or support a union, or to bargain collectively with a representative of their choosing.

“We train our managers to comply with labor law and respect the rights of our employees,” the spokesperson told Banking Dive via email. “In this case, the majority of eligible employees freely voted against a union in a Board supervised secret ballot election and the facts do not support allegations to the contrary.”

Wells Fargo is cooperating with the investigation but believes these allegations are unfounded and plans to defend the company and employees, the spokesperson added.

An NLRB hearing before a judge is scheduled for October, and Wells Fargo, if ordered to collectively bargain, can appeal to NLRB members in Washington, Bloomberg reported.

Recently, unionized Wells Fargo employees hit a new challenge in organizing. The bank's conduct management intake team won its union vote 21-16 in December, making it the first non-branch unit at Wells Fargo to unionize.

The team, which handles customer and employee complaints across various locations, has now filed an unfair labor practice charge with the NLRB through Wells Fargo Workers United-CWA. The complaint alleges that the bank illegally refuses to engage in collective bargaining following the certified union vote, American Banker reported. However, the bank contends it’s waiting for the outcome of the NLRB’s review and claims there were procedural flaws in the handling of the vote.

CWA unionized 24 Wells Fargo branches last year, with around 200 employees being organized.

Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf pushed back on employee unionization efforts last April, saying it’s important to “make clear that we continue to believe that our employees are best served by working directly with Wells Fargo and our leadership team.”

#7726. Help set the ABA’s new advocacy agenda in D.C.: Take the Legislative Priorities Survey

The ABA is inviting all members to help set its advocacy priorities for the 120th Congress through the ABA Legislative Priorities Survey. (Al Drago/Bloomberg)

The historic November midterm elections have rewritten the political landscape in Washington, D.C., setting the stage for Democratic control of both chambers of Congress and a potentially consequential legislative agenda.

The 120th Congress convenes in early January to confront the challenges of governing in a divided government. It is important that the American Bar Association is ready to engage and to have a strong voice at the table on issues affecting the legal profession and the administration of justice. As a new balance of political power takes shape during President Donald Trump’s final two years in office, the ABA is inviting all members to help set its advocacy priorities for the 120th Congress through the ABA Legislative Priorities Survey.

Participation in the survey is available exclusively to ABA members. By participating in the survey, you have the opportunity to have your voice heard on issues that matter most to the legal profession and the justice system.

The survey opened Nov. 6 and will close on Dec. 4. Most ABA members have received an email with a personalized link to the survey. But any member can access the survey at ambar.org/priorities. Members can also expect an invitation from ABA President Barbara Howard, and the link will be distributed via the ABA’s social media. With a new political landscape taking shape in Washington, the ABA Legislative Priorities Survey will play an important role in ensuring that the association’s advocacy efforts reflect the concerns and priorities of our members.

The 2026 survey has an even more streamlined ranking system than the last priorities survey. Members are being asked first to prioritize issues aligned with the ABA’s current priorities and policies. Members then respond to open-ended questions designed to identify additional policy issues the ABA should consider prioritizing, including those that might require the development of new policies.

The survey takes less than 10 minutes to complete, and your input will be indispensable to informing the ABA’s legislative priority-setting process.

The survey results will be presented to the Board of Governors at the ABA Midyear Meeting in early 2027. The Board will consider ABA member input, along with the following criteria, to determine whether an issue should be made a priority:

• Breadth and strength of the ABA interest • Importance to the practice of law • Public perception of the profession • Opportunity for impact • Potential for achievement • Timeliness of issue • Expertise of lawyers on the issue • Importance to society • Importance to the administration of justice

The 120th Congress presents new opportunities for the ABA to advance policies important to our members and our legal profession and to work with policymakers as they contend with issues that could have far-reaching consequences for our nation.

#7718. Russell Brand sentenced to 10 years following rape and sexual assault conviction

British comedian, actor and podcaster Russell Brand arrives at the Southwark Crown Court in London during his trial on charges of rape, sexual assault and indecent assault. He was convicted and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison. (Photo from Shutterstock)

British comedian and actor Russell Brand was sentenced in London on Monday to 10 years and six months in prison following his conviction for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.

High Court of England and Wales Judge Joel Bennathan described Brand, 51, as a sexual predator who used his public standing to shield himself from accountability before women came forward following media reports in 2023, Courthouse News Service reports.

Brand will likely serve two-thirds of his sentence before being released on parole, the judge said. The sentencing followed a four-week trial in which jurors found Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Before the sentencing, the court heard victim impact statements from the women, who described the lasting effects of the attacks on their confidence, relationships and ability to feel safe.

The judge considered Brand’s charitable work, including helping people struggling with addiction by funding treatment. However, he said good character and exemplary conduct would not normally justify a significant reduction in a prison sentence.

#7711. Sheriff allows law firm to profit from policing, lawsuit alleges

Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz at a U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging hearing in Washington, D.C., on April 30, 2025. (Photo by Annabelle Gordon/Sipa USA/Sipa via AP Images)

In a lawsuit that could affect how some forfeitures are handled in Florida, the Miami-Dade County sheriff is being accused of unconstitutionally allowing a law firm to profit when police seize property and cash.

Under federal and state forfeiture law, police departments can seize money or assets, such as boats, that they think were used in crimes or purchased with ill-gotten gains.

Mobile phone distributors and retailers in Miami argue that a firm run by Israel “Izzy” Reyes—a former cop, a former prosecutor and a former judge—is representing the sheriff’s office in civil forfeiture cases and keeping 20% to 35% of the proceeds, plus an additional 5% on appeal.

According to court papers filed in October, the companies said their bank accounts were frozen last year, and more than $45.2 million was seized as as part of civil forfeiture cases handled by the firm.

An additional $2.6 billion has also been targeted for seizure, the companies alleged, according to a story by the Miami Herald.

Rosie Cordero-Stutz is the first elected sheriff in Miami-Dade County since the 1960s.

#7710. Florida Man Sentenced for Stealing Millions of Dollars from Lenders Using Sham Cosmetic Surgery Clinics and Stolen Identities

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Today, A Wellington, Florida, man was sentenced today to 84 months in prison for using sham cosmetic surgery clinics and the stolen identities of more than 100 people to defraud medical lenders of approximately $2.3 million, and for fraudulently seeking COVID-19 disaster relief loans.

“Jacquez Tullis built fake medical clinics using stolen identities, including those of practicing doctors and deceased individuals, and used them to steal millions from lenders,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. “When the pandemic hit, Tullis then tried to exploit taxpayer-funded relief meant for struggling small businesses. Today’s sentence makes clear that the Fraud Division will hold accountable those who abuse the public’s trust, whether they steal from private lenders or from the American people.”

“The defendant’s actions represent a serious breach of trust, exploiting the identities of innocent individuals and manipulating financial institutions for personal gain,” said Special Agent in Charge Brett D. Skiles of FBI Miami. “Fraud schemes of this magnitude undermine the integrity of our financial system and inflict real harm on victims whose identities are stolen and misused. The FBI remains committed to protecting the American public, holding accountable those who exploit others for financial gain, and pursuing those who believe they can hide behind elaborate schemes.”

According to court documents and admissions in his plea, from approximately April 2018 through February 2024, Jaquez Tullis, 42, and his co-conspirators created six sham medical clinics that claimed to offer cosmetic surgery and other medical services, but provided no real care.  The conspirators registered the clinics with the Florida Department of State using stolen personal identifying information of practicing doctors and others without their knowledge or consent.  In some cases, they listed those doctors as clinic owners on applications to become approved merchants with six medical lenders.  Those lenders, two FDIC-insured banks and four financial technology companies financed out-of-pocket procedures not covered by insurance.

Once the clinics were approved, the conspirators submitted fraudulent credit card applications to the lenders in the names of more than 100 individuals, seeking approximately $3.1 million.  The applications falsely represented that the funds were for cosmetic surgery and other services the clinics would provide.  In fact, the individuals did not know about or authorize the applications and did not need or want any treatment. According to death records, some had died before the dates they supposedly received care.

Separately, from April through August 2020, Tullis submitted at least nine fraudulent applications on behalf of certain businesses to the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) for Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) loans, a federal stimulus program authorized as part of the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act.  Tullis obtained funds under EIDL program by submitting false and fraudulent loan applications that collectively sought $696,860 in EIDL funds. The loan applications falsely represented, among other things, the business’ number of employees and revenue.

Tullis pleaded guilty on July 21, 2026, to conspiracy to commit bank fraud and aggravated identity theft.

U.S. District Judge Rodolfo A. Ruiz, II, of the Southern District of Florida sentenced Jacquez Dion Tullis, to 60 months on the bank fraud conspiracy count and a consecutive 24 months on the aggravated identity theft count, for a total of 84 months in prison, to be followed by 5 years of supervised release. Tullis was also ordered to pay $2,309,859.44 in restitution, $200 in special assessment, and forfeiture money judgement of $2,309,859.44

Two co-defendants were previously sentenced:

All three defendants were charged as part of the Justice Department’s 2025 National Health Care Fraud Takedown, announced on June 30, 2025.

Trial Attorney Shana Priore of the Fraud Division’s Public Trust and Financial Integrity Section prosecuted the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Sandra Demirci of the Southern District of Florida handled asset forfeiture.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

#7707. The SEC has requested to delay climate rule arguments. What’s next?

Sustainable investing experts are not surprised by the delay and say it is expected to have minimal immediate impact.

Acting Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Mark Uyeda’s decision last week to ask the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals to delay arguments for the agency’s climate risk disclosure rule did not come as a surprise to regulatory experts in the space.

While the change is expected to have minimal immediate impact, it sets the stage for a shift in focus for the SEC under the Trump administration.

The SEC issued its long-awaited climate-risk disclosure rule last March, nearly two years after it was first proposed — and amid over 24,000 public comments. Uyeda was one of two commissioners to vote against the rule’s approval. The rule was immediately met with multiple lawsuits that were later consolidated into the Eighth Circuit. The spate of legal challenges led the agency to stay the rule’s implementation in April.

Given the agency’s stay and the change in administration, Tom Willman, regulatory lead for artificial intelligence sustainability platform Clarity AI, said Uyeda’s decision came “as no great surprise.”

“It is nevertheless disappointing that investors will be deprived of much-needed financially material information related to climate related risks,” Willman said by email Wednesday.

Julie Gorte, senior vice president of sustainable investing at Impax Asset Management was more blunt in an interview: “The only person on the planet who didn't see this coming was Rip Van Winkle,” she said Wednesday.

Uyeda’s recommended pullback on defending the SEC climate rule follows his prior critiques of the rule. During the hearing on the final climate rule, in the weeks after it was finalized and in his Feb. 11 statement announcing the delay request, Uyeda maintained his belief that the SEC does not have the authority to promulgate the rule or require such disclosures.

Jenner & Block Partner Jennifer Lee, a former assistant director of the SEC Enforcement Division, said Uyeda’s position is “consistent with the new, Republican-led SEC’s shift back to focusing on ‘bread and butter’ investor disclosure issues.” Lee, who now represents companies and financial institutions in regulatory investigations and litigation, told ESG Dive in emailed comments Thursday that she expects that focus to include an emphasis on materiality, while looking to avoid “overly prescriptive disclosure requirements for public companies.”

The change in SEC posture, however, is expected to have a minimal impact for companies or investors, according to Willman and Gorte.

“The impact of this is going to be extraordinarily minimal, partly because it was never enforced in the first place,” Gorte said Wednesday. “So we never had better climate reporting stimulated by U.S. regulatory postures to begin with. And for U.S. companies, or for any company really, a lot of the big ones are probably still going to have to be reporting on all the same things that were in that rule because of [other jurisdictions].”

Willman echoed that note and said that many U.S. companies already voluntarily report climate risks due to investor demand, in addition to growing regulatory requirements both overseas in jurisdictions like the European Union, and stateside in California. New York recently reintroduced its own version of California’s climate disclosure laws.

Additionally, Stephen O’Day, a partner at Smith, Gambrell & Russell, noted the intervenors in the case could continue the rule’s defense, even though the SEC’s announcement indicates this iteration of the agency is not inclined to defend the rules. In the case of the climate rule, 18 states and the District of Columbia have signed on as intervenors to support the agency’s rule.

O’Day said a similar process happened after intervenors continued the defense for enforcement actions taken by the Clinton-era administration for violations of the Clean Air Act by coal-fired plants. Ultimately, the intervenors prevailed, and the Supreme Court upheld the actions.

“The proceedings pending in the Eighth Circuit involve challenges filed by multiple parties and intervenors, any of which could seek to continue defense of the SEC rules,” O’Day said. “So, while the court may grant the requested 45-day pause, it remains to be seen whether any such pause will result in the end of the SEC’s final rules.”

Regardless, sustainability programs and disclosures are expected to continue.

“Regulatory shifts don’t change the fundamental reality: physical climate risk is already priced into markets,” Lukky Ahmed, CEO of climate risk data and analytics platform Climate X, said by email Wednesday. Firms have a fiduciary responsibility to continue to assess, manage and disclose climate risks to their operations, Ahmed said.

“Integrating climate resilience and adaptation strategies isn’t just prudent — it’s essential for maintaining business performance, driving shareholder returns, and protecting communities," Ahmed said.

Despite the shifting federal policy stance, “there is a lot of faith that the drivers of sustainability remain in place no matter who is in anyone's White House,” Gorte told ESG Dive.

“If we don't solve the climate crisis, there are going to be … parts of the globe that are probably uninhabitable, or where people can't work outdoors in the summer. If we don't solve the biodiversity crisis, the prospects are even worse.” Gorte said. “So there are things that we have to do in order to preserve what we think of as life as we know it, and those drivers are going to remain in place.”

#7705. Top Dallas County investigator arrested, charged with wife’s murder

Jimmy Harold Spurger Jr., 54, the chief investigator for the Dallas County public defender’s office, was arrested and charged with first-degree murder Saturday after his wife was found dead in their apartment. (Photo from the Dallas County Sheriff’s Department)

The chief investigator for the Dallas County public defender’s office was arrested and charged with first-degree murder Saturday after his wife was found dead in their apartment.

Jimmy Harold Spurger Jr., 54, who has worked for the public defender’s office for nearly 14 years, was married to his wife, Maria Teresa Spurger, for 35 years but filed for divorce in late October, according to Fox 4.

Local first responders who were conducting a welfare check Friday night forced their way into the apartment, where they found Spurger’s wife unresponsive on a couch with a knife in her neck, Fox 4 reports. Spurger also was found in the apartment, covered in blood and sitting next to a knife in the bedroom.

After responding officers found multiple pill bottles also covered in blood, they suspected that Spurger had ingested pills and transported him to the hospital, Fox 4 reports. He was later taken into custody and is being held on a $1 million bond.

Spurger has led the Investigative Division for the Dallas County public defender’s office for 11 months, Fox 4 reports. Previously, he spent more than 13 years in its Capital Murder Division. He also worked for more than 20 years in law enforcement, which included supervising investigations in the Child Abuse and Family Violence Division of the Dallas County district attorney’s office.

Dallas County Chief Public Defender Christi Dean told Fox 4 that Spurger was “an exemplary colleague,” and that “it’s hard to imagine that he has been charged with murder.”

“We know in our profession that the probable cause affidavit doesn’t tell the whole story,” Dean also reportedly said. “The media reports don’t tell the whole story. And we’re still in preliminary stages.”

#7702. DEI attacks are likely to refine and improve programs, experts say

The intense pressure to end diversity initiatives has led companies to scrutinize their policies. Many of the attacks will end up strengthening DEI programs.

The politicians, provocateurs and think tanks that in the past few years have worked to dismantle diversity, equity and inclusion may not appreciate the full consequences of their efforts.

They’ve used a variety of tactics, in the public and private sectors, including White House executive orders; lawsuits or the threat of lawsuits; shareholder proposals; and needling on social media. They’ve notched high-profile wins, most notably the Supreme Court’s ruling against affirmative action and capitulation at several companies, including retailers and brands that have ended or scaled back their DEI programs.

The successful challenges, inevitably, are forcing scrutiny of DEI practices. But they also provide an opportunity to reinforce DEI goals and execution, which David Glasgow, executive director of New York University’s Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion, and Belonging, sees as a silver lining.

Indeed, the victories are hardly universal. Because diversity, equity and inclusion are good for business for a variety of reasons, most companies are not abandoning DEI. So far in 2025, Target, Nike and Costco are among those that have defended at least some aspects of their policies (in Costco’s case, vociferously). As the Heritage Foundation, a major DEI foe, noted in November, most Fortune 500 companies continue to publicly commit to DEI.

“It is a time for companies to refine and strengthen their inclusion efforts in ways that reduce the risk in the short term — because the risk is real, and we know that — and in ways that are sustainable in the long term,” said Adrienne Pulido, vice president of inclusion insights at Kantar. “So it is looking at both ends of the spectrum, in terms of being very clear about what inclusion means to their business.”

DEI is being pilloried as discriminatory and unfair, yet these systems are designed to create a business that is neither. That is, a business where employees have a variety of backgrounds and perspectives (diversity); hiring, promotion and other actions are executed fairly (equity); and the culture is comfortable and inviting to all who work there (inclusion).

“Unpacking what DEI is and what inclusion is, is part of this moment we're in and part of the conversation that companies need to have about their strategies,” Pulido said by video conference. “What does DEI mean to the business itself? What does it mean to the business and to the future business? Because the demographics of the country are changing, and our research shows that inclusion as a concept, as an idea, is very popular among Americans of all backgrounds.”

DEI goals for most companies are more important than ever because the markets for their products and services are more diverse than they were a decade or more ago, according to Effenus Henderson, who has worked in recruiting, staffing and succession planning at companies in the U.S. and abroad since the 1970s.

“This attack is amplified through the use of social media and technology and psychometrics, where emotions get aroused and reinforced,” he said by phone. “But fundamental to all this is that DEI is not about creating systems that are discriminatory, or about quotas, or a focus on one thing at the exclusion of others. I don't think organizations have really done that. What they have been doing is really trying to expand participation because of the growing demographic change that we're seeing.”

The need to develop DEI strategies that fit with and further business strategies dictates the involvement of leadership, according to Henderson. Too often, though, they are left to the human resources department, leaving companies at risk of adopting DEI programming that is ineffective and possibly indefensible.

“The companies that are able to navigate this generally are the ones where leadership has spent the time talking about it,” he said. “It's not just about reacting to the George Floyd situation or to civil rights laws or litigation. It's really, ‘How do we integrate this as a part of the DNA of who we are as an organization?’ If your organization is more performative, then they don't really understand how it helps to shape business strategy and policy.”

DEI should be treated like any other strategic priority, according to Tim Heneveld, country director for Pergolux in North America. With DEI under the spotlight, it’s a good moment to reassess whether hiring, workplace environment, leadership and operational strategies fit with broader aims.

“That means setting measurable goals, using data to track impact, and holding leadership accountable,” Heneveld said by email. “Some organizations are feeling pressure to scale back DEI, but I think doing so would be shortsighted. Instead, companies should refine their DEI strategies, aligning them with long-term business goals rather than reacting to what they are seeing in the media or any other outside factors. I've experienced, firsthand, workplaces can attract top talent, strengthen their teams, and improve retention.”

In some cases, companies are continuing with their DEI efforts, but changing the names of their initiatives or titles of their employees, experts said.

Crafting DEI initiatives and training is always a work in progress because businesses, markets and demographics evolve, according to Henderson. For many companies, that may mean avoiding those three letters of the alphabet, or the words “diversity, equity and inclusion.” But that, too, requires some thought, he said.

“Is continuing to refer to it under those banners still appropriate, and if I look at renaming it, am I doing that to help enhance our appeal to the markets of the customers and employees we serve? Are we doing it as a reactive, defensive thing for a short-term issue that's hot and heavy right now?” he said. “Get clarity around your objectives, the alignment with your strategies, and then decide whether how you are framing it today will work for you tomorrow and the day after. At some companies, it may mean one thing, and to others it may mean something else.”

The list of lawsuits against DEI programs tracked by the Meltzer Center is long, and getting longer.

Most of these claims invoke civil rights laws intended to end or prevent unfair hiring practices or contracts. Frequently that includes Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, barring discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin; Section 1981 of the federal code barring discrimination in contracts; and the U.S. Constitution’s equal protection clause, according to Glasgow. The Meltzer Center advises companies to avoid DEI practices that give preference to members of certain groups and involve a tangible benefit.

Evaluating whether a company’s DEI programs run afoul of the latest interpretations of these codes entails enlisting attorneys or other compliance experts.

“This has become a thriving legal practice area,” Glasgow said.

Any business strategy should always be grounded in risk mitigation, and this is just another place for companies to check, according to Henderson. Companies may learn that, to avoid risk, certain aspects of their DEI programs should change.

Others may find that they pass muster. In its proxy statement urging shareholders to vote against a proposal that could have weakened its DEI programs, Costco’s board of directors made clear that the retailer regularly evaluates its “practices concerning compliance with law, including evolving Supreme Court decisions.”

In describing how Costco obeys the law and does not discriminate in hiring, promotion and other practices, the board also provided a litany of protected statuses. This is a reminder that, while civil rights statutes are being leveraged to overturn DEI practices, they nevertheless do bar discrimination for a host of reasons. Moreover, any company that does business abroad will encounter antidiscrimination law that isn’t being disrupted by political activism the way it is in the U.S., Henderson said.

“If you look at Canada, Europe, Asia and South America, there are regulations and laws that support and value diversity,” he said. “So backing away from DEI may, in fact, create harm for your business strategies in other parts of the world. It's not a simple answer, and it just depends on who you are.”

While it may seem like DEI programs are quickly getting scrapped in order to avoid controversy, most are simply under review, Glasgow and others said.

“I think it's prompting a much deeper reflection within companies, not just on what is strictly legal or illegal in what we're doing, but on what has been working and what has not been working,” Glasgow said. “Could we be doing this work more effectively, in a way that actually helps us achieve our business goals, or helps us create the kind of culture that we want to create? Are there things that have been low impact, or maybe even have a negative impact, that we should get rid of, even if it's not for legal reasons? I think the moment that we're living in now could be a helpful reset moment for the field.”

#7694. Who Is Elena Kagan? Ideology, strategy, and the art of disagreement

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

On May 21, 2026, Justice Elena Kagan did something she had never done in nearly 16 years on the Supreme Court: she dissented alone in a signed decision. The case, Havana Docks v. Royal Caribbean Cruises, concerned whether cruise lines could face liability for using Cuban docks confiscated decades earlier. Eight justices, including Kagan’s liberal colleagues Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson, sided against the cruise lines. Kagan thought the majority had misunderstood a basic principle of property law: the interest originally confiscated had expired long before the cruise ships arrived.

The solitary dissent was unusual for a justice who has spent much of her tenure avoiding separate opinions. At a judicial conference in July 2025, Kagan observed that the court “speaks best when it speaks as a court,” and acknowledged that she sometimes drafts dissents only to decide against publishing them.

Kagan’s professional background is also unusual. She is the only current justice who arrived at the Supreme Court without previously serving as a judge. Before her appointment in 2010, she had been a law professor, dean of Harvard Law School, a White House adviser, and solicitor general of the United States. Her career was therefore shaped substantially by institutions in which persuasion, negotiation, and managing competing perspectives are routine.

But how much does this explain her jurisprudence? Ideological measures generally place Kagan to the right of her liberal colleagues, and her voting record contains meaningful differences from Sotomayor’s and Jackson’s. Yet those differences are far from uniform, and Kagan’s reluctance to write separately persists even when she reaches precisely the same result as her colleagues.

Understanding Kagan therefore requires examining not only how she votes, but how she chooses to agree and disagree.

Kagan has generally occupied a position to the right of the other liberal justices in measures of Supreme Court ideology. But the distance between them depends considerably on how ideology is measured, which cases are examined, and when the comparison is made.

The best-known measure is the Martin–Quinn score, which estimates the justices’ ideological positions from their voting patterns over time. In the 2024-25 term, Kagan’s score was −1.85, compared with −2.80 for Jackson and −4.19 for Sotomayor. Kagan was thus the rightmost of the three liberals, although she remained substantially to the left of the court’s median justice, Amy Coney Barrett, whose score was +0.53. The estimates for Jackson and Kagan had been closer in earlier terms (and, in fact, Jackson was initially positioned slightly to Kagan’s right).

The scores capture something revealing about how the justices vote, but they do not directly measure the substance of their legal reasoning or their willingness to compromise. Nor does a justice’s location relative to the other liberals necessarily reveal whether her own jurisprudence has changed. Martin–Quinn estimates are relative positions derived from voting coalitions, and those coalitions are themselves influenced by the court’s membership and docket.

The voting record offers a more concrete comparison. During the 2010–2021 terms, there were 56 contested decisions in which Kagan joined the majority while Sotomayor dissented, compared with just 19 in which their positions were reversed. Kagan was nearly three times as likely to be on the prevailing side when the two disagreed. That is a substantial difference, although it does not establish that every disagreement reflected an ideological division.

Justice Stephen Breyer, long considered a moderate liberal on the court, provides a useful point of reference. During their overlapping time on the court, Kagan joined the majority without Breyer 41 times, while Breyer joined the majority without Kagan 31 times. The more balanced relationship suggests that Kagan’s historical voting behavior often resembled Breyer’s more closely than Sotomayor’s.

The picture has changed since Jackson joined the court in 2022. Across 121 contested decisions in which Kagan and Sotomayor both participated through the 2025 term, they voted on the same side 109 times. Kagan prevailed without Sotomayor seven times, while Sotomayor prevailed without Kagan five times. Their historical difference in majority participation has thus narrowed dramatically.

The convergence is particularly visible in closely divided cases. Of 82 decisions decided 5–4 or 6–3 in which Kagan, Sotomayor, and Jackson all participated, the three liberals voted together in 71. When the court divided most sharply, Kagan usually found herself alongside her liberal colleagues rather than occupying a position between the liberal and conservative wings.

There are then two different stories in the numbers. Over much of her tenure, Kagan was more likely than Sotomayor to support outcomes favored by conservative justices. More recently, that distinction has diminished, particularly in closely divided cases. Whether this reflects a change in Kagan’s jurisprudence or the changing opportunities for cross-ideological agreement remains uncertain.

The cases in which she breaks with her liberal colleagues offer a way to examine that distinction more closely.

One way to identify a comparatively moderate justice is to examine how frequently she votes with colleagues across the ideological divide. By that measure, Kagan has demonstrated considerable independence from her liberal colleagues.

Across 26 terms, Kagan was the only liberal voting alongside conservative justices in 27 contested decisions, approximately 5.3% of her non-unanimous votes. Sotomayor occupied that position in 18 decisions, or 3.4%. Yet Breyer did so in 29 cases, representing 7.1% of his contested votes during the years he served alongside Kagan. When he was on the court, Breyer, rather than Kagan, was more likely to separate from the other liberals in that way.

The pattern becomes even more interesting with Jackson’s arrival. During the 2022–2025 terms, Kagan was the sole liberal voting with conservatives in nine contested cases, compared with ten for Jackson (though this frequency has decreased) and just two for Sotomayor. Jackson’s cross-ideological votes were evenly divided between joining majorities and dissents, while Kagan’s predominantly placed her in the majority. Thus, even when two justices cross ideological lines with similar frequency, they may not be doing the same thing.

These voting coalitions also raise a question about Kagan’s reputation as a consensus-builder. Does she actually attract more conservative support when writing for the court?

The analysis provides surprisingly little evidence that she does. Of Kagan’s 47 majority opinions in contested decisions, 27 attracted at least three conservative votes. Sotomayor achieved the same result in 30 of her 49 contested majority opinions. Their records are then similar, suggesting that Kagan’s reputation for building agreement is not necessarily reflected in a distinctive ability to assemble ideologically diverse majorities.

The individual cases also complicate the idea that Kagan’s departures from the liberal wing are simply strategic compromises. In 2020’s Kahler v. Kansas, for example, Kagan wrote for six justices, including five conservatives, holding that the Constitution does not require states to recognize an insanity defense based on a defendant’s inability to distinguish right from wrong. Breyer, joined by Ginsburg and Sotomayor, dissented. Kagan emphasized the historical diversity of insanity rules and the latitude afforded to state legislatures; Breyer saw Kansas’s approach as eliminating a fundamental protection deeply rooted in criminal law.

Four years later, Pulsifer v. United States presented a dispute over the meaning of a single conjunction in a federal sentencing statute. Kagan wrote for a six-justice majority, including five conservatives, adopting a reading that restricted defendants’ eligibility for relief from mandatory minimum sentences. Gorsuch dissented, joined by Sotomayor and Jackson, favoring an interpretation that would have made relief more widely available.

Neither case is easily explained as Kagan merely accommodating conservative colleagues and both show substantive disagreements over the meaning of legal rules, with significant consequences for criminal defendants.

These decisions also show why ideological distance and judicial method cannot be treated as interchangeable. Kagan’s cross-ideological votes sometimes reflect legal commitments that produce outcomes different from those favored by her liberal colleagues. They also suggest that her willingness to build agreement does not automatically lead her toward the narrowest available resolution.

If Kagan is not consistently more successful than Sotomayor at attracting conservative votes, the more distinctive feature of her jurisprudence may lie elsewhere: what she does after reaching agreement, and particularly when she decides that a disagreement warrants an opinion of her own.

The art of agreement: choosing when to write

The most distinctive feature of Kagan’s judicial behavior may have less to do with how she votes than with how she expresses agreement. During her 16 terms on the court, Kagan authored just 18 concurrences in signed decisions, compared with 81 for Sotomayor. Breyer, often described as an institutionally minded pragmatist, also wrote concurrences at more than twice Kagan’s rate during their overlapping service. Jackson has been considerably more prolific in her shorter tenure. Kagan’s comparative restraint is therefore striking even among justices who share many of her substantive positions.

The difference becomes even more revealing when the comparison is limited to cases in which the justices reached exactly the same outcome. Between 2010 and 2021, Kagan and Sotomayor both supported a conservative-authored majority opinion in 93 contested decisions. Sotomayor wrote separately in 13 of those cases; Kagan did so in just one. The difference is difficult to explain through ideology or case selection alone: the two justices were participating in the same decisions, agreeing with the same majorities, yet approaching the question of whether to write separately very differently.

The distinction has narrowed somewhat in recent years, but it has not vanished. During the 2022–2025 terms, Kagan wrote separately in three of 38 conservative-authored majorities she shared with Sotomayor, compared with five for Sotomayor. In 29 comparable cases involving Kagan and Jackson, Kagan wrote separately twice and Jackson eight times. These samples are smaller, but they reinforce the larger finding that Kagan is particularly reluctant to add her individual voice to an outcome she already supports.

Kagan herself has offered a remarkably candid explanation for this. Speaking at the 9th Circuit Judicial Conference in July 2025, she described the Supreme Court as an institution whose opinions should communicate a collective judgment. She acknowledged that producing a single institutional voice requires “a little bit of flexibility and compromise.” Separate opinions, she suggested, can complicate the law by presenting competing explanations of what the court has supposedly decided.

Yet Kagan’s restraint should not be mistaken for unqualified agreement. In 2024’s United States v. Rahimi, she joined Roberts’ majority upholding a federal restriction on firearm possession by individuals subject to certain domestic violence restraining orders. She also joined Sotomayor’s concurrence, which defended the majority’s application of New York State Rifle & Pistol Association Inc. v. Bruen while reiterating their disagreement with that earlier Second Amendment decision holding there to be a constitutional right to carry a firearm. Jackson wrote her own concurrence addressing the difficulties lower courts had encountered applying Bruen. All three liberals agreed with the outcome, but their choices about authorship differed.

A similar pattern appeared in 2023’s National Pork Producers Council v. Ross, in which the court rejected an argument by pork producers that a law violated the Constitution by regulating the pork industry outside of California. Kagan joined Sotomayor’s separate opinion explaining why they agreed with the judgment without embracing portions of Gorsuch’s reasoning that threatened to alter the established constitutional framework. Kagan was willing to register a qualification, but she did so by joining a colleague’s opinion rather than writing another.

These distinctions again complicate the portrayal of Kagan as a consensus-builder. The data do not show that she consistently attracts more conservative support to her own majority opinions than Sotomayor does. They show something different: Kagan is considerably more selective about articulating separate disagreements when she already supports the court’s disposition. That behavior may preserve a clearer institutional message, but it also leaves fewer public indication of her reservations about particular decisions.

The difference matters when interpreting Kagan’s ideological position. A justice who joins an opinion without writing separately may appear closer to its author than one who publishes a concurrence, even when both share the same substantive objection. Kagan’s record suggests the absence of a separate opinion can reflect a decision about judicial expression rather than any lack of disagreement.

The limits of agreement: textualism, precedent, and dissent

Kagan’s willingness to work across ideological lines has never meant avoiding deep disagreements with the court’s conservatives. Some of her sharpest opinions have challenged not only their conclusions but also their fidelity to the interpretive principles they profess to follow.

In a 2015 lecture at Harvard Law School honoring Antonin Scalia, Kagan famously remarked, “We’re all textualists now.” The observation acknowledged Scalia’s influence on statutory interpretation, including among justices who did not share his ideological commitments. Seven years later, in her dissent in West Virginia v. EPA, Kagan explicitly revisited that statement: “It seems I was wrong.”

Her objection concerned the majority’s use of the major questions doctrine to restrict the Environmental Protection Agency’s authority under the Clean Air Act. Kagan argued that the court had departed from ordinary statutory interpretation by demanding an unusually clear congressional authorization for agency action of substantial economic or political significance. In her account, the conservative majority’s claimed commitment to textualism yielded when the statutory text pointed toward an outcome it disfavored.

The exchange is revealing because Kagan was challenging the majority from within a methodology often associated with conservative jurisprudence. Her embrace of textualism did not entail agreement with the conservatives about what particular statutes meant, much less about how much authority courts should exercise over Congress and administrative agencies.

That distinction became even clearer in 2024’s Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. Writing for the three liberals, subject to Jackson’s recusal in one of the consolidated cases, Kagan defended Chevron deference (deferring to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes) against the majority’s decision to overrule it. Her argument rested on statutory interpretation, congressional allocation of authority, administrative expertise, and the importance of precedent (a common theme for her). Textualism, in Kagan’s jurisprudence, does not necessarily require courts to resolve every statutory ambiguity without deference to an agency authorized to administer the law.

The same institutional concerns appear in her criticism of the court’s emergency docket. In Trump v. Wilcox, Kagan dissented from an order permitting the administration, pending further litigation, to remove officials from independent agencies. Joined by Sotomayor and Jackson, she objected both to the treatment of longstanding precedent and to the use of an expedited proceeding to alter the practical operation of existing law without ordinary briefing and argument.

These opinions provide an important counterweight to Kagan’s reputation for accommodation. Her restraint in writing separately does not preclude forceful disagreement when she believes the court has departed from established interpretive or institutional principles. Nor does that pattern necessarily distinguish her substantive positions from those of Sotomayor and Jackson, who joined these dissents.

The recurring question is therefore not simply whether Kagan is willing to compromise but where she draws the line between disagreements she can accommodate and those that she considers important enough to articulate publicly.

Sixteen years of decisions reveal a justice whose reputation for moderation captures only part of her judicial behavior. Kagan has historically been more willing than Sotomayor to join conservative-supported outcomes, and some of those differences reflect genuine disagreements about the law. Yet the gap has narrowed considerably in recent terms, particularly in cases that divide the court along ideological lines.

What distinguishes Kagan more consistently is her approach to disagreement. She is not uniquely successful at attracting conservative votes to her majority opinions. Rather, she is unusually reluctant to write separately when she can support an existing opinion, even in cases where her liberal colleagues reach the same result but feel compelled to explain their reservations. Her willingness to join another justice’s concurrence further complicates any assumption that silence necessarily signifies agreement.

The distinction has become more consequential as the court has moved rightward. Kagan’s opportunities to assemble majorities across ideological lines have diminished, while her dissents in disputes over administrative authority, precedent, and institutional power have become an increasingly public part of her jurisprudence.

Whether those patterns reflect a conscious strategy, enduring professional instincts, or some combination of the two cannot be determined from voting records alone. But the comparisons suggest that understanding Kagan requires looking beyond where she falls on an ideological scale. Her place on the court is defined both by the legal positions she takes and by the choices she makes about when – and how – to express them.

Dr. Adam Feldman is the creator and author of the blog Empirical SCOTUS and the Substack Legalytics.

Recommended Citation: Adam Feldman, Who Is Elena Kagan? Ideology, strategy, and the art of disagreement, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 5, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/who-is-elena-kagan-ideology-strategy-and-the-art-of-disagreement/

#7693. Lindsay Clancy loses bid to dismiss murder case with retrial possibility

Lindsay Clancy was being tried for first-degree murder. She admitted to killing her three children and claimed that she suffered from postpartum psychosis. (Photo by CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via the Associated Press)

Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse charged with strangling and killing her three small children in 2023, lost her bid to have her case dismissed Monday, setting the stage for a possible retrial.

Massachusetts Superior Court Judge William Sullivan’s 17-page ruling found that a retrial would not be considered double jeopardy because Clancy’s initial jury was deadlocked.

Clancy, 36, was on trial earlier this year for the strangling deaths of her three young children. The case ended in a mistrial after one juror, known as “Juror Doe,” held out for a conviction. Clancy pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, alleging that she was going through postpartum psychosis at the time of the tragedy, according to coverage on Courthouse News Service.

Last week, a hearing seeking dismissal of the case explored the role of Michael Desronvil, who is referred to as “Juror Doe” in court records. Desronvil was accused of not following the court’s instructions.

Sullivan found that the evidence “did not reasonably suggest Juror Doe’s inability to deliberate or refusal to follow the law.”

On Nov. 2, the prosecution said it intends to try Clancy again. She initially faced three counts of murder for the deaths of Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months.

#7690. Judge halts CFPB firings

In the same order, the bureau was told not to delete any agency data or transfer its reserve funding to the Fed or anywhere else. The CFPB then reportedly placed most workers on administrative leave.

A federal judge has ordered the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and its acting director, Russ Vought, not to terminate any agency employee except for cause related to job performance or conduct until March 3, when another hearing in the case will take place.

The bureau responded, however, by placing on administrative leave all employees except those asked to return to work by “the Acting Director, Chief Legal Officer, or another designee,” according to an email from the CFPB’s human capital operations manager that was seen by Bloomberg Law.

The court order on Friday came after the National Treasury Employees Union urged Judge Amy Berman Jackson on Thursday to block Vought from a “mass firing” it believed would affect 95% of the bureau’s workforce as early as Friday.

In the same Friday order, Berman Jackson demanded that the CFPB “not delete, destroy, remove, or impair” any data or agency records covered by the Federal Records Act.

Berman Jackson also ordered the CFPB and Vought not to transfer money from the bureau's reserve funds, other than "to satisfy” the agency’s “ordinary operating obligations.” That includes returning money from the CFPB’s reserve funds to the Federal Reserve, as Vought said this month he would do.

The data-related developments follow a declaration the CFPB’s former chief technologist, Erie Meyer, filed with the court Friday, warning that databases holding 12 years’ worth of information the agency has collected would soon be deleted and “irretrievably lost.”

Affected data would include “supervisory and examination records of financial institutions, enforcement action data, consumer complaints, personal consumer information, and market research records,” Meyer wrote.

Loss of data that tracks institutions’ financial behavior “would impair the Bureau's ability to identify risks and respond to emerging threats within the financial system,” Meyer wrote.

“This could destabilize markets, allow bad actors to exploit weaknesses in financial institutions, and undermine public trust in the financial system,” she wrote.

It would also open the financial system to market manipulation, Meyer asserted.

“Tech companies moving into financial services could gain an illegal competitive advantage by accessing sensitive consumer financial data or enforcement records, and the audit logs of that activity could be deleted,” she wrote. “This could result in unfair competition and undermine market integrity.”

That may serve as a reference to X Money, the payments tool set for launch this year in a partnership between card network Visa and social media platform X, owned by Trump adviser Elon Musk, who’s also seen as the architect behind the Department of Government Efficiency, which infiltrated the CFPB this month.

The deletion of CFPB data “would leave consumers without critical recourse in the event of financial harm caused by institutions under the Bureau's jurisdiction,” Meyer wrote. Further, she asserted, it would make the CFPB’s Consumer Response database “unavailable and/or unreliable, severely hamper — if not entirely take down — the Bureau’s website, and likely result in the loss of mandatory public reporting the Bureau has previously done.”

Friday’s order may represent a relief to CFPB employees, but it doesn’t apply to bureau employees who have already been terminated. The agency last Tuesday terminated roughly 70 probationary employees, then Thursday fired another 70 to 100 term employees – those whose contracts have set limits between one and four years.

Altogether, last week’s firings cut roughly 10% of the CFPB's workforce, according to American Banker.

The CFPB was not the only banking regulator to see workforce reductions last week. Roughly 500 employees at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., or about 8% of its workforce, accepted a deferred resignation offer from the Trump administration, Bloomberg Law reported Friday, citing a spokesperson for the agency.

The FDIC then terminated probationary employees, the outlet reported Monday, though the number of employees affected remained unclear.

An FDIC spokesperson on Friday did not detail how deeply certain units of the regulator were affected.

A lawyer representing the CFPB workers’ union laid out the urgency of Friday’s court action.

”I’m asking that they don't fire the entire agency tonight,” Deepak Gupta, a founding principal at Gupta Wessler, told the court, according to American Banker. “I don’t want to leave the courthouse without some assurance that the mass layoff is not going to happen and then become a fait accompli.”

The workers’ union asked Thursday for a temporary restraining order to stop the firings, but agreed to seek a preliminary injunction instead.

That mirrors a case in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, in which the city of Baltimore sued the CFPB, claiming Vought’s move to return the agency’s funding to the Fed would effectively shut down the bureau “by fiat.”

The government agreed Thursday that Vought would refrain from transferring money out of the CFPB’s reserve fund or returning money to the Fed or Treasury until Feb. 28, or upon a “contrary order” from the court, Bloomberg Law reported.

Still, in the workers’ union case, Brad Rosenberg, a Justice Department special counsel, objected to the request for a preliminary injunction.

"We don't think any preliminary relief is appropriate at this stage because we don't think the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits," he said, according to American Banker.

Among the employees the CFPB terminated Thursday is Julia Barnard, who served as the agency’s student loan ombudsman since last February. Her position is mandated by the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act.

“This work matters,” Barnard said in a statement issued by the Student Borrower Protection Center. “It’s a lifeline for borrowers and a safeguard against a system that too often fails them. Dismantling this function is unconscionable and will cost real people real money.”

Delaying any further moves to slash the CFPB workforce would at least give employees time to plan and budget for their personal futures. Employees of the agency are entitled by law to 60 days’ notice of job loss. But last week’s firings came with no notice and with immediate effect.

Further, terminations for cause (probationary employees, for example, were notified that they were deemed “not fit for continued employment because [their] ability, knowledge and skills do not fit the Agency’s current needs”) left those employees without access to severance, one lawyer with the CFPB told ABC News.

In Vought’s first week as the CFPB’s acting director, the bureau’s headquarters were closed to employees, who were ordered to stop all bureau work. A tip line was also set up for people to report on employees who might be conducting work.
